title: Why plain speech serves the many
english: In beginning this sixth book against the charges Celsus brings against Christians, holy Ambrose, what we need to contend with in it is not, as one might suppose, the passages from philosophy he sets out. For Celsus has quoted a good many passages, chiefly from Plato, and has set beside them passages from the sacred writings that could win over even an intelligent reader, claiming that these things were said better among the Greeks, and without the lofty pretension and the claim that they come from God or from a Son of God.

We say, then, that if the aim of those who champion the cause of truth is to benefit as many people as they can and, out of love for humankind, to bring to the truth, as far as possible, everyone whatever, not only the quick-witted but also the dull, and again not Greeks only while leaving out the barbarians (and it is a great civilizing work if a man is able to turn even the most boorish and unlearned), then it is clear that he must also take care to speak in a style that benefits all and is able to draw every hearer.

But those who have bidden a long farewell to the unlearned, as if they were slaves unable to follow the train of thought set out in literary phrasing and arrangement, and have cared only for those brought up in letters and learning, have narrowed what they share with others into a very small and narrow compass.

title: Power from God, not polished words
english: I have said this in defence of the plain diction of the Scriptures, for which Celsus and others accuse them, a plainness that seems to be eclipsed by the brilliance of artful composition. For our prophets, and Jesus and his apostles, had in view a way of speaking that not only contains the truth but is also able to draw the many, until, encouraged and led in, each according to his capacity rises to the things spoken in hidden ways in words that seem plain.

And if I must make bold to say it, the very beautiful and studied diction of Plato and of those who wrote in a similar way has benefited few, if it has benefited anyone at all; but the diction of those who taught and wrote more plainly, and at the same time with an eye to the substance and to the many, has benefited more. At any rate, one can see that Plato is in the hands only of those who are thought to be lovers of letters, while Epictetus is admired even by ordinary people who have an inclination toward being helped, since they sense the improvement that comes from his words.

And we say this not to find fault with Plato (for the great world of humankind has usefully produced him too), but also to show the meaning of those who said: “My word and my preaching were not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that our faith might not rest on the wisdom of men but on the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:4–5). The divine word says that what is spoken, even if it is true in itself and most persuasive, is not enough to reach a human soul unless some power is also given from God to the speaker and grace blooms upon what is said; and this grace too does not come without God to those who speak to good effect. So the prophet says in the sixty-seventh Psalm (Psalm 68 in English Bibles): “The Lord will give a word to those who bring good news with great power” (Psalm 68:11).

So, granting that in some cases the same doctrines are held by the Greeks and by those of our teaching, they still do not have the same power to win souls and to shape them according to those doctrines. That is why the disciples of Jesus, unlearned as far as Greek philosophy is concerned, travelled through many nations of the world, shaping each of their hearers according to his worth, as the Word willed; and these hearers, in proportion to the inclination of their free will toward accepting the good, became much better.

title: Plato knew the truth, yet was without excuse
english: Let the wise men of old, then, make things known to those able to understand them; and let Plato, the son of Ariston, indicate in one of his letters what concerns the first good, and say that the first good can by no means be “spoken”, but that it arises “from long association” and appears “suddenly, like a light kindled from a leaping fire, in the soul” (Plato, Seventh Letter 341c–d). When we hear these words we too agree with them as well said, “for God showed them” (Romans 1:19) these things and whatever else has been well said.

This is why we say that even those who have grasped the truth about God, but have not practised the worship of God that is worthy of the truth about him, are liable to the punishments of sinners. For Paul says of such people in so many words: “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men who hold the truth in unrighteousness, because what can be known of God is plain among them, for God showed it to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made, both his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse; because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasonings, and their senseless heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds and four-footed beasts and creeping things” (Romans 1:18–23).

So those people do indeed “hold the truth”, as our own word also bears witness, who think that the first good “can by no means be spoken”, and say that “from long association with the matter itself, and from living with it, suddenly, like a light kindled from a leaping fire, it comes to be in the soul and from then on nourishes itself” (Plato, Seventh Letter 341c–d).

title: Philosophers who saw God and worshipped idols
english: Yet those who wrote such things about the first good go down “to the Piraeus” to pray to Artemis as a goddess and to watch the festival held by the common people (Plato, Republic 1.327a). After philosophizing so loftily about the soul and describing the life of the soul that has lived well, they abandon the greatness of what “God showed them” (Romans 1:19) and think mean and petty thoughts, paying “a cock to Asclepius” (Plato, Phaedo 118a). And though they pictured to themselves “the invisible things” of God and the ideas “from the creation of the world” and from the things of sense, from which they ascend to the things known by the mind, and though they saw, not ignobly, his eternal power and divinity, they nonetheless “became futile in their reasonings” (Romans 1:20–21), and their “senseless heart” (Romans 1:21), as it were, wallows in darkness and ignorance about the worship of the divine.

And one can see men who pride themselves on their wisdom and their theology bowing down to “the likeness of an image of corruptible man” (Romans 1:23), in honour, so it is said, of that being, and sometimes even going down with the Egyptians to birds or four-footed beasts or creeping things. And even if some seem to have risen above these things, they will still be found to have “exchanged the truth of God for a lie” and to be worshipping and serving “the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25).

Therefore, since the wise and learned among the Greeks go astray in their deeds concerning the divine, “God chose” “the foolish things of the world” “to put the wise to shame”, “and the base things” “and the weak things” “and the things despised”, and “the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are” (1 Corinthians 1:27–28); and truly, so that “no flesh may boast before God” (1 Corinthians 1:29).

But our own wise men, Moses, the most ancient of all, and the prophets after him, were the first to know that the first good can “by no means” be “spoken”. They did write, since God shows himself to those who are worthy and fit, that God “appeared”, for example, to Abraham or to Isaac or to Jacob (Genesis 12:7; Genesis 26:24; Genesis 35:9; Exodus 6:3). But who it was that appeared, and of what kind, and in what manner, and to which part of us, they have left to be examined by those able to make themselves like the men to whom God appeared; for he was seen not by their bodily eyes but by their pure heart. For, according to our Jesus, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

title: The light kindled in the soul
english: That a “light” is kindled “in the soul” “suddenly, as from a leaping fire” (Plato, Seventh Letter 341c–d), the Word knew first, saying in the prophet: “Light for yourselves the light of knowledge” (Hosea 10:12). And John, who lived after him, says that “what came to be” in the Word “was life, and the life was the light of men” (John 1:3–4); and this “true light” “enlightens every man coming into the” true and intelligible “world” (John 1:9), and makes him “a light of the world” (Matthew 5:14). For this light “shone in our hearts to give the light of the gospel of the glory of God in the face of Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6; 2 Corinthians 4:4).

That is why a most ancient prophet, who prophesied many generations before the reign of Cyrus (for he was more than fourteen generations older than Cyrus), says: “The Lord is my light and my saviour; whom shall I fear?” (Psalm 27:1); and: “Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Psalm 119:105); and: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4:6); and: “In your light we shall see light” (Psalm 36:9). And the Word in Isaiah, urging us toward this light, says: “Be filled with light, be filled with light, Jerusalem; for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (Isaiah 60:1). And this same prophet, prophesying of the coming of Jesus, who turns people away from the worship of idols and images and demons, says: “To those who sat in the region and shadow of death a light has risen” (Isaiah 9:2; Matthew 4:16); and again: “The people who sat in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2; Matthew 4:16).

See, then, the difference between what Plato said well about the first good and what is said in the prophets about the light of the blessed. And see that the truth about this in Plato did nothing to help his readers toward pure piety, nor even the man himself who philosophized in such terms about the first good; whereas the plain diction of the divine writings has filled with divine inspiration those who read it sincerely. In such readers this light is nourished by the oil spoken of in a certain parable, the oil that kept the light of the torches burning for the five wise virgins (Matthew 25:1–13).

title: Things too great to be written
english: Celsus also sets out another passage from Plato’s letter, which runs as follows: “If it had seemed to me that these things could be adequately written and spoken for the many, what finer thing could I have done in my life than to write what is of great benefit to humankind and to bring nature to light for all?” (Plato, Seventh Letter 341d). So let us discuss this too, briefly. Whether Plato had something more sublime than what he wrote, and more divine than what he left behind, or not, we leave to each person to examine as best he can. But we show that our prophets too had in mind certain things greater than what is written, which they did not write down.

For Ezekiel receives a roll “of a book”, written “in front” and behind, in which there was “lamentation and song and woe” (Ezekiel 2:9–10); and at the command of the Word he eats the book, so that he might not write it down and betray it to the unworthy (Ezekiel 3:1–3). John too is recorded to have seen and done something similar (Revelation 10:9–10). And Paul too “heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter” (2 Corinthians 12:4). And Jesus, who is greater than all of these, is said to have “spoken” the word of God “to the disciples” “privately” (Mark 4:33–34), especially in times of retreat; but what he said has not been recorded. For it did not “seem” to them that these things “could be adequately written for the many” or “spoken”.

And if it is not tasteless to tell the truth about such great men, I say that these men saw better than Plato, from the thoughts they received by the grace of God, which things are “to be written” and how they are “to be written”, and which are by no means “to be written for the many”, and which are “to be spoken” and which are not of that kind. And again John, teaching us the difference between what is to be written and what is not, says that he heard seven thunders teaching him about certain things and forbidding him to commit their words to writing (Revelation 10:3–4).

title: The prophets did not borrow from Plato
english: Many things could also be found in Moses and the prophets, who are older not only than Plato but even than Homer and than the invention of letters among the Greeks, things worthy of the grace God gave them and filled with greatness of mind. These men did not, as Celsus supposes, say such things because they had misheard Plato. For how could they have heard a man who had not yet been born?

And even if someone applies Celsus’s argument to the apostles of Jesus, who lived later than Plato, consider whether it is not unbelievable on the face of it to say that Paul the tentmaker (Acts 18:3), Peter the fisherman (Matthew 4:18), and John, who left his father’s nets (Matthew 4:21–22), handed down such teaching about God because they had misheard what Plato said in his letters.

Celsus has already harped many times on the charge that people are required to believe at once, and now he says it again as if it were something new beside what he said before. What we have said in answer to this is enough for us.

Since he also sets out another passage of Plato, in which he says that wisdom shines out upon those who practise philosophy in Plato’s way “when they use questions and answers” (Plato, Seventh Letter 344b), come, let us show from the sacred writings that the divine word also urges us toward dialectic. In one place Solomon says, “Instruction left unexamined goes astray” (Proverbs 10:17); in another Jesus son of Sirach, who left us the book called Wisdom, says, “The knowledge of the senseless man is unexamined talk” (Sirach 21:18). So it is rather among us that kindly refutations are found, among those who have learned that the one who presides over the word must be able “to refute those who contradict” (Titus 1:9).

But if some are careless, and do not train themselves to attend to the divine readings, to “search the Scriptures” (John 5:39), and, as Jesus commanded, to seek the meaning of the Scriptures, to ask God about them, and to knock at what is shut in them (Matthew 7:7), the word is not for that reason empty of wisdom.

title: Greek wonder-tales and Plato’s oath
english: Then, after other passages of Plato showing that the good is known to “few,” because the many, filled “with a contempt that is not right” and “with a lofty and empty hope,” speak of certain things as true “as though they had learned something grand” (Plato, Seventh Letter 341e), he says that Plato, though he had said this beforehand, still does not tell tales of wonder, nor does he stop the tongue of anyone who wishes to weigh what it is that he professes, nor does he bid people believe straight away: “God is of such a kind, and he has a Son of such a kind, and this Son came down and talked with me.”

To this I reply that Aristander, I think, wrote of Plato that he was not the son of Ariston but of an apparition that came to Amphictione in the form of Apollo; and many other Platonists have said such things in their accounts of Plato’s life. And as for Pythagoras, who told a great many marvels, who showed his ivory thigh at a festival gathering of the Greeks, who claimed he recognized the shield he had used when he was Euphorbus, and who is said to have appeared in two cities on one day, what need is there even to speak?

Anyone who wants to charge that tales of wonder are told about Plato and Socrates will cite the swan that was presented to Socrates in a dream, and the teacher who said, when the young man was presented to him, “So this was the swan.” He will also take up as a tale of wonder the third eye that Plato saw he himself had. Malicious people, who wish to speak evil of what has appeared to those who stand above the many, will never lack slander and abuse; they will also mock the divine sign of Socrates as a fiction.

We, then, are not telling tales of wonder when we relate the things about Jesus, and his true disciples did not write such stories about him. But Celsus, who professes to know everything and quotes many passages of Plato, deliberately, I think, keeps silent about the teaching on the Son of God that is stated by Plato in the letter to Hermias and Coriscus. Plato’s words run thus: “and swearing by the God of all things, leader of what is and of what is to be, Father and Lord of the ruling principle and cause; whom, if we truly practise philosophy, we shall all know clearly, as far as is possible for blessed human beings” (Plato, Sixth Letter 323d).

title: Plato’s steps to knowledge and Christ
english: Celsus also sets out another passage of Plato, which runs thus: “It has come into my mind to speak still more at length about these matters, for perhaps what I am speaking of would become clearer once this has been said. There is a true argument that stands against anyone who has dared to write anything at all on such subjects; I have often stated it before, yet it seems it must be stated now as well. Each of the things that exist has three things through which knowledge must come; the fourth is knowledge itself; and as a fifth one must set the thing itself, which is knowable and true. Of these, the first is the name, the second the word, the third the image, and the fourth knowledge” (Plato, Seventh Letter 342a–b).

Along the same lines we might say that John, “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1:23; Isaiah 40:3), was brought in before Jesus, corresponding to the name in Plato; and that second, after John, comes Jesus, pointed out by him (John 1:29), to whom the words “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14) apply, corresponding to the word in Plato.

Plato calls the third the image. But since we give the name “image” another use, we will say more plainly that the imprint of the wounds that forms in the soul after the word is the Christ in each person, coming from Christ the Word. And whether Christ, the wisdom that is “among the mature” on our side (1 Corinthians 2:6; 1 Corinthians 1:24), also corresponds to the fourth, which is knowledge, let anyone who is able consider.

title: Faith with reasons, suited to each hearer
english: Then he says: “You see how Plato, though he has firmly declared that it cannot be ‘spoken,’ nevertheless, so as not to seem to take refuge in what cannot be examined, gives a reasoned account of this difficulty; for perhaps even ‘nothing’ could be ‘spoken.’” But since he brings this forward to establish that one must not simply believe but must give a reasoned account of what is believed, we too shall use the saying of Paul that rebukes the one who believes rashly, in which he says, “unless you believed rashly” (1 Corinthians 15:2).

As far as it rests with him, Celsus, by repeating himself, forces us to repeat ourselves. After the boasts he has already described, as though they were the boasts of impostors, he says that Plato does not boast and lie by claiming that he himself has discovered something new, or that he has come from heaven to announce it, but admits where these things come from.

Anyone who wished to answer Celsus might say in reply that Plato too boasts, in the speech of Zeus in the Timaeus, where he says, “Gods of gods, whose maker and father I am” (Plato, Timaeus 41a), and the rest. But if someone defends these words by appeal to the meaning of the Zeus who makes the speech in Plato, why should not one who examines the meaning of the words of the Son of God, or of the Creator’s words in the prophets, say something even greater than the speech of Zeus in the Timaeus? For what marks out divinity is the foretelling of things to come, things spoken not by the power of human nature and shown by their outcome to have been announced by a divine Spirit.

So we do not say to everyone who comes to us, “First believe that the one I am introducing to you is the Son of God.” Rather, we bring the word to each person in the way that suits his character and condition, for we have learned “to know how we ought to answer each one” (Colossians 4:6). There are some to whom we preach this, since they can do no more than be urged to believe; to others we come, as far as we can, with proof by way of questions and answers.

Nor do we say what Celsus said in mockery: “Believe that the one I am introducing to you is the Son of God, even though he was bound in the most dishonourable way or punished in the most shameful way, even though only yesterday or the day before he was knocked about most disgracefully before the eyes of all.” Nor do we say, “For this reason believe all the more.” For on each of these points we try to say even more than we have set out above.

title: Only one Son of God has been preached everywhere
english: After this Celsus says: “If these men” (he means the Christians) “introduce one, and others another, and the common and ready word of them all is ‘Believe, if you want to be saved, or go away,’ what will those do who truly want to be saved? Will they throw dice to divine where to turn and whom to join?”

To this too we shall say, starting from what is plain to see: if there had been several who, like Jesus, were recorded to have come into human life as sons of God, and each of them had drawn some people away to himself, so that, because their claims were alike, it was disputed whether the one attested by those who believe in him was the Son of God, then there would be room for the words “If these men introduce one, and others another, and the common and ready word of them all is ‘Believe, if you want to be saved, or go away,’” and the rest. But as it is, Jesus has been preached throughout the whole inhabited world as the only Son of God who has come to the human race.

For those who, like Celsus, supposed that wonders had been invented, and who therefore wanted to invent wonders in the same way, thinking that they too would gain the same mastery over people, were shown to be nothing: Simon, the Samaritan magician, and Dositheus, who came from the same country as he. For the one claimed that he was the power of God that is called great (Acts 8:10), and the other that he too was the son of God.

Indeed, nowhere in the inhabited world are there Simonians. And yet Simon, in order to win more followers, took away from his disciples the danger of death, which Christians have been taught to choose, by teaching them to treat idolatry as a matter of indifference. But not even at the beginning were the Simonians plotted against; for the evil demon who plots against the teaching of Jesus knew that none of his own purposes would be undone by the teachings of Simon. The Dositheans did not flourish even in earlier times, and now they have died out entirely, so that their whole number is reported to be not even thirty.

Judas the Galilean too, as Luke wrote in the Acts of the Apostles, wanted to call himself someone great, and before him Theudas; but since their teaching was not from God, they were destroyed, and “all who obeyed” them were at once scattered (Acts 5:36–39). So we do not throw dice to divine where to turn and whom to join, as though there were several who could draw us away with the claim that they had come from God to the human race. But enough about these things.

title: Celsus traces the saying on worldly wisdom to the Greeks
english: So we pass on to another charge of Celsus. He does not even know our actual words, but from scraps he has misheard he said that we say “the wisdom among men is foolishness with God,” although what Paul says is: “The wisdom of the world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19). Celsus says that the reason for this has been given already. He thinks the reason is that by this saying we want to win over only the uneducated and the stupid. But, as he himself noted, he said the same thing earlier, and we have answered that argument as well as we could. Even so, he wanted to show that this too was made up by us and taken from the wise men of the Greeks, who said that human wisdom is one thing and divine wisdom another.

He does indeed set out sayings of Heraclitus: one in which he says, “For human character has no insight, but divine character has” (Heraclitus, fragment 78 DK), and another, “A man is called an infant by a divinity, as a child is by a man” (Heraclitus, fragment 79 DK). He also sets out these words from the Apology of Socrates written by Plato: “For I, men of Athens, have gained this name through nothing else than wisdom. What sort of wisdom is this? The kind that is perhaps human wisdom; for in truth I may well be wise in that” (Plato, Apology 20d).

These, then, are the passages Celsus sets out. I will add these as well, from Plato’s letter to Hermias, Erastus and Coriscus: “To Erastus and Coriscus I say, old as I am, that besides this fine wisdom of the Forms they still need a wisdom that guards against wicked and unjust men, and a certain power of self-defence. For they lack experience, because they have spent much of their life with us, who are moderate men and not bad ones. That is why I said they still need these things, so that they may not be forced to neglect the true wisdom and to attend to the human and necessary kind more than they should” (Plato, Letter 6, 322d–e).

title: Divine wisdom, knowledge and faith
english: According to these passages, then, there is a divine wisdom and a human one. The human is what we call “the wisdom of the world,” which is “foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19). But the divine, which differs from the human, if it is indeed divine, comes by the grace of God, who gives it to those who have made themselves fit to receive it, and above all to those who know how each wisdom differs from the other and therefore say in their prayers to God: “For even if one is perfect among the sons of men, yet if the wisdom that comes from you is absent, he will be counted as nothing” (Wisdom of Solomon 9:6).

We say that human wisdom is a training ground for the soul, and divine wisdom its goal. Divine wisdom is also called the “solid food” of the soul by the one who said: “But solid food is for the mature, for those whose faculties have been trained by practice to distinguish good from evil” (Hebrews 5:14).

This view is truly ancient, but its antiquity does not go back, as Celsus thinks, to Heraclitus and Plato. For before them the prophets drew the distinction between the two kinds of wisdom. For the present it is enough to quote from the words of David what is said of the man who is wise with divine wisdom: he “will not see corruption,” David says, “when he sees the wise dying” (Psalm 49:9–10).

Divine wisdom, then, which is different from faith, is the first of what are called the “gifts” of God (1 Corinthians 12:4). After it, second, for those who know how to be exact in such matters, comes what is called knowledge; and third, since the simpler people too, who come to godliness as best they can, must be saved, comes faith. That is why Paul says: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:8–9). So you would find that it is not ordinary people who have a share in divine wisdom, but those who rise above and excel all who hold to Christianity; nor does anyone expound the matters of divine wisdom to the most uneducated, or to slaves, or to the most ignorant.

title: Who are truly the uneducated
english: It is true that Celsus calls one set of people “most uneducated and slaves and most ignorant”: those who do not know his precepts and have not been schooled in the learning of the Greeks. We, however, call most uneducated those who are not ashamed to talk to lifeless things, who call on what is weak for health, ask what is dead for life, and beg what is most helpless for help (Wisdom of Solomon 13:17–18). And even if some say that these things are not the gods but imitations and symbols of the true ones, these too are none the less uneducated and slaves and ignorant, since they imagine that imitations of the divine are in the hands of common craftsmen. So we say that even the least among us have been freed from this lack of education and this ignorance, and that the divine hope is understood and grasped by the most intelligent.

We also say that it is impossible for one who has not been trained in human wisdom to take in the more divine wisdom; and we confess that all human wisdom is foolishness compared with the divine. Then, when he ought to argue the point, he calls us charlatans and says that we flee headlong from the more cultivated, since they are not ready to be deceived, and lure in the more rustic like birds. For he did not see that from the very beginning our wise men were schooled in outside learning as well: Moses “in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:22), and Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael in all the learning of the Assyrians, so that they were found ten times better than all the wise men there (Daniel 1:4, 17, 20). Even now the churches have, in proportion to their numbers, few wise men who have come to them from what we call wisdom “according to the flesh” (1 Corinthians 1:26); but they also have those who have passed from that wisdom to the divine wisdom.

title: Humility, Plato’s and ours
english: Next, Celsus, like someone who has heard talk of humility at second hand and has not taken the trouble to understand it, wants to speak ill of the humility we teach, and thinks it a mishearing of Plato’s words. Plato says somewhere in the Laws: “God, as the ancient saying has it, holding the beginning, the end and the middle of all things that are, goes straight to his end as he moves round according to nature. And Justice always follows him, the avenger of those who fall short of the divine law; and he who is to be happy holds fast to her and follows, humble and well-ordered” (Plato, Laws 4.715e–716a). Celsus does not see that, among men far more ancient than Plato, these words were spoken in prayer: “Lord, my heart was not lifted up, nor were my eyes raised high; nor did I walk among great things, nor among wonderful things above me, unless I was humble-minded” (Psalm 131:1–2).

At the same time these words show that the humble-minded man does not necessarily humble himself in an unseemly and degrading way, falling to the ground on his knees and throwing himself face down, putting on the clothes of the wretched and heaping dust on himself. For the man who is humble-minded as the prophet describes walks “among great and wonderful things” above him (Psalm 131:1), among doctrines that are truly “great” and thoughts that are truly “wonderful,” and he humbles himself “under the mighty hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6). If some, through lack of learning, have not grasped clearly the teaching on humility and act in this way, the teaching is not to blame; rather we should pardon the lack of learning in those who have set the better things before themselves but, through their simplicity, fail to reach them.

For more truly “humble and well-ordered” than Plato’s humble and well-ordered man is the one who is well-ordered because he walks “among great” and “wonderful things” above him, and humble because, even while among these, he humbles himself of his own will, not under just anyone but “under the mighty hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6), through Jesus, the teacher of such lessons, who “did not count being equal with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave,” and “being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:6–8). So great is the teaching on humility that its teacher is no ordinary one, but our Saviour himself, great as he is, says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29).

title: The camel and the eye of the needle
english: After this he takes the pronouncement of Jesus against the rich, when he said, “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Matthew 19:24), and says that it was plainly borrowed from Plato, and that Jesus corrupted Plato’s saying where Plato said that “for one who is exceptionally good to be exceptionally rich as well is impossible” (Plato, Laws 5.742e–743a).

Who with even a moderate power to weigh the facts, not only among those who believe in Jesus but among the rest of mankind as well, would not laugh at Celsus on hearing that Jesus, who was born and brought up among the Jews, who was thought to be the son of Joseph “the carpenter” (Luke 3:23; Matthew 13:55), and who had not learned letters, not only those of the Greeks but not even those of the Hebrews (John 7:15), as the truth-loving writings about him also testify, read Plato, and, pleased with his saying about the rich, that “it is impossible to be exceptionally good and rich,” corrupted it and turned it into “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Matthew 19:24)?

If Celsus had loved the truth, and had not read the Gospels with hatred and hostility, he would have considered why a camel was chosen for comparison with the rich man, an animal crooked in its build; and what Jesus meant by the narrow “eye of the needle” (Mark 10:25), since he says that the way that leads “to life” is narrow and hard (Matthew 7:14); and the fact that in the law this animal is recorded as “unclean,” having something acceptable, in that it chews the cud, but also something to be blamed, in that it does not part the hoof (Leviticus 11:4; Deuteronomy 14:7). He would also have examined how often the camel is mentioned in the divine Scriptures, and in connection with whom, so as to see the intent of the saying about the rich. Nor would he have left unexamined the fact that Jesus calls the poor blessed and the rich wretched (Luke 6:20, 24): whether these words of his […] refer to the poor and the rich as the senses perceive them, or whether the Word knows a poverty that is wholly blessed and a wealth that is wholly to be blamed. For not even an ordinary person would praise the poor without discrimination, since most of them are of very bad character. But enough of this.

title: God hidden in darkness, made known by the Son
english: Next, wishing to belittle what is written among us about the kingdom of God, he quotes none of it, as if it were not even worth recording in his book (perhaps because he did not even know it), but sets out passages of Plato from the Letters and the Phaedrus, as though these were spoken by divine inspiration, while our writings have nothing of the kind. Come, then, let us set a few of ours beside them, for the sake of comparison with what Plato said. His words are not unpersuasive; yet they did not lead the philosopher to conduct himself in a way worthy at least of himself in his piety toward the Maker of all things, a piety he ought not to have adulterated or defiled with what we call idolatry, or, to use the word most people would use, superstition.

In a Hebrew manner of speaking, then, it is said of God in the seventeenth Psalm (Psalm 18 in English Bibles) that “God made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 18:11). This is said to show that what could be worthily conceived about God is hidden and unknown, since he has hidden himself, as it were, in darkness from those who cannot bear the flashing brightness of the knowledge of him and cannot see him: partly because of the defilement of the mind, bound as it is to a human “body of humiliation” (Philippians 3:21), and partly because of its too limited power to comprehend God.

And to show that the knowledge of God reaches human beings rarely and is found in very few, Moses is recorded to have entered “into the thick darkness where God was” (Exodus 20:21). And again it is said of Moses: “Moses alone shall come near to God, but the rest shall not come near” (Exodus 24:2). And again, to present the depth of the teachings about God, a depth beyond the grasp of those who do not have the “Spirit” who searches all things, and searches “even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10), the prophet said: “The abyss, like a garment, is his covering” (Psalm 104:6).

Our Saviour and Lord too, the Word of God, shows the greatness of the knowledge of the Father: that the Father is grasped and known as he deserves first of all by the Saviour alone, and secondarily by those whose ruling faculty is enlightened by the Word and God himself. He says: “No one has known the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son reveals him” (Matthew 11:27). For no one can know the uncreated one, the firstborn of all created nature (Colossians 1:15), as he deserves, as the Father who begot him knows him; nor can anyone know the Father as his living Word, his Wisdom and Truth, knows him. It is by sharing in the Word that whoever has the capacity to know the Father knows him, since the Word takes away from the Father what is called the “darkness” that he “made his hiding place” and what is called his “covering,” the abyss, and in this way reveals the Father.

title: Something holier than Plato’s King of all
english: I thought it right to set out these few things, out of the very many that holy men have conceived about God, to show that the sacred writings of the prophets hold something more majestic than the Platonic sayings Celsus admired, for those whose eyes are able to see the majesty of the Scriptures.

The passage of Plato that Celsus set out runs as follows: “All things are about the King of all, and all things are for his sake, and that is the cause of all beautiful things. The second is about the second things, and the third about the third. The human soul, then, longs to learn about them, what sort of things they are, looking to what is akin to itself, none of which is adequate. But concerning the King and the things I have spoken of, there is nothing of that kind” (Plato, Second Letter 312e–313a).

I could have set out what is written in Isaiah about those the Hebrews call “seraphim,” who cover the “face” and the “feet” of God (Isaiah 6:2), and about those named “cherubim,” whom Ezekiel described (Ezekiel 10:1–22), and their forms, so to speak, and in what way God is said to ride upon the cherubim (Psalm 18:10). But since these things are said in a very hidden way, because of the unworthy and the irreverent, who cannot follow the grandeur and majesty of theology, I did not think it fitting to discuss them in this treatise.

title: The place above the heavens was sung before Plato
english: Next after this Celsus says that some Christians, having misunderstood the words of Plato, boast of “the God above the heavens,” climbing up past “the heaven of the Jews.” Here he does not make clear whether they climb past the God of the Jews as well, or only past the heaven by which the Jews swear. It is not our task now to speak about those who proclaim another God besides the one whom the Jews also worship; our task is to defend ourselves and to show that the prophets of the Jews whom we accept cannot have taken anything from Plato, for they were older than he.

So we did not take from Plato the saying “All things are about the King of all, and all things are for his sake.” We have learned from the prophets things said better than these, since Jesus and his disciples made plain the meaning of the Spirit who was in the prophets, who was none other than the Spirit of Christ (1 Peter 1:11). Nor is the philosopher the first to set forth what concerns the place above the heavens. Long ago David set forth the depth of the many insights about God that belong to the realms beyond the things of sense, when he said in the book of Psalms: “Praise God, you heavens of heavens, and the water that is above the heavens; let them praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:4–5).

For my part, I do not rule out that Plato learned the words in the Phaedrus from certain Hebrews and, as some have recorded, had even come upon the prophetic writings when he set them out. There he said: “The place above the heavens no poet here below has ever yet sung, nor ever will sing, as it deserves,” and what follows (Plato, Phaedrus 247c), among which is this too: “For the being that truly is, colourless, shapeless and intangible, visible only to mind, the pilot of the soul, the being with which the true kind of knowledge is concerned, holds this place” (Plato, Phaedrus 247c).

And our Paul, trained by those very prophetic words, longing for what lies beyond the world and beyond the heavens and doing everything for its sake, that he might attain it, says in the Second Letter to the Corinthians: “For our momentary light affliction is working out for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory, as we look not at what is seen but at what is not seen; for what is seen is temporary, but what is not seen is eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:17–18).

title: Seeing the unseen beyond the heavens
english: For to those able to hear he states it plainly, calling the things of sense “what is seen,” and naming the intelligible things, grasped by the mind alone, “what is not seen.” He also knows that the things of sense, the things “seen,” are “temporary,” and that the intelligible things, the things “not seen,” are “eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18). And since he wished to be engaged in contemplating those things, helped by his longing for them he counted every affliction as nothing and as something light. In the very time of “affliction” and toil he was in no way weighed down by them; because of his contemplation of those things he made light of every hardship.

For we too have “a great high priest,” who by the greatness of his power and of his mind “has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God” (Hebrews 4:14). He has promised those who have truly learned divine things and have lived worthily of them that he will lead them on to what lies beyond the world. For he says: “so that where I am going, you also may be” (John 14:3).

For this reason we hope, after the toils and the contests here, to reach the very heights of the heavens. Having received, according to the teaching of Jesus, springs of “water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:14), and having made room for rivers of contemplation (John 7:38), we hope to be with the waters said to be “above the heavens,” which praise “the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:4–5). And as long as we praise him, we shall not be carried round by the revolving of heaven, but shall always be engaged in contemplating the invisible things of God, no longer understood by us “from the creation of the world through the things that are made” (Romans 1:20), but as the true disciple of Jesus put it, when he said, “but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12), and, “when what is perfect comes, what is partial will be done away” (1 Corinthians 13:10).

title: Not seven heavens, but Jacob’s ladder
english: The Scriptures in use in the churches of God do not speak of seven heavens, or of any fixed number of them at all, but of “heavens”; and their words seem to teach either the spheres of what the Greeks call the planets or something else more secret.

Celsus, following Plato, says that the road for souls to the earth and from the earth passes through the planets. But Moses, our most ancient prophet, says that a divine dream was seen by our patriarch Jacob: a ladder reaching “to heaven,” and angels “of God” going up and coming down on it, and the Lord resting firmly at its top (Genesis 28:12–13). In his account of the ladder Moses was hinting either at these same things or at something greater than these. Philo too has written a book about this ladder, which deserves thoughtful and intelligent study by lovers of truth.

title: Celsus parades the mysteries of Mithras
english: After this, Celsus, wishing to display his wide learning in his treatise against us, also sets out certain Persian mysteries, where he says: “These things are hinted at also by the teaching of the Persians and by the rite of Mithras that is among them. For in it there is a symbol of the two revolutions in heaven, that of the fixed stars and that assigned in turn to the planets, and of the soul’s passage through them. The symbol is this: a ladder with seven gates, and on top of it an eighth gate. The first of the gates is of lead, the second of tin, the third of bronze, the fourth of iron, the fifth of alloyed coin-metal, the sixth of silver, and the seventh of gold. The first they assign to Kronos, taking the lead as a sign of the slowness of that star; the second to Aphrodite, likening to her the brightness and softness of tin; the third to Zeus, the bronze-floored and solid one; the fourth to Hermes, for iron and Hermes alike endure every kind of work, make money, and toil hard; the fifth to Ares, the gate of mixed metal, uneven and varied; the sixth, the silver one, to the Moon; the seventh, the golden one, to the Sun, imitating their colours.”

Next he examines the reason for the stars being listed in this order, which is shown by symbols in the names of the rest of the materials, and he attaches musical ratios to the Persian theology he sets out. Not content with this, he takes pains to set out a second explanation as well, again bound up with musical theory.

But it seemed to me absurd to set out Celsus’s words on these matters. It would be like what he himself has done: in his accusation against Christians and Jews he brought in, out of season, not only the teachings of Plato, when he might have been content with those, but also what he calls the Persian mysteries of Mithras and their explanation. For however these things stand for those who honour the rites of Mithras and for the Persians, whether falsely or truly, why did he set out these rather than one of the other mysteries along with its explanation? For among the Greeks the mysteries of Mithras are not thought to be anything special compared with the Eleusinian mysteries, or with the rites of Hecate handed down to those initiated in Aegina.

And if he wanted to set out barbarian mysteries with their explanation, why not rather those of the Egyptians, in which many take pride, or those of the Cappadocians about the Artemis at Comana, or those of the Thracians, or even those of the Romans themselves, who initiate the noblest members of the Senate? But if he thought it out of place to bring in any of those, as contributing nothing to his accusation of Jews or Christians, how did the same thing not seem out of place to him when he set out the Mithraic rites?

title: Scripture’s own gates and camps
english: But suppose someone wished to find starting points for a more mystical contemplation of how souls enter into divine things, not in the very obscure sect that he cited, but in books partly Jewish, read in their synagogues and accepted by Christians as well, and partly belonging to Christians alone. Let him read the visions seen by the prophet at the end of the prophecy of Ezekiel, in which different gates are described, hinting at something about the different ways in which more divine souls enter upon better things (Ezekiel 40–48). Let him read also, in the Revelation of John, what is said about the city of God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and about its foundations and its gates (Revelation 21:2, 10–21; compare Hebrews 12:22).

And if he is able to learn also the way, shown through symbols, of those who will journey to divine things, let him read the book of Moses entitled Numbers, and let him look for someone able to initiate him into what is written there about the camps of the sons of Israel (Numbers 2:1–31): which are drawn up on the east side as first, which toward the southwest or the south, which toward the sea, and which are last, toward the north. For he will see in these passages contemplations not to be despised, and not, as Celsus supposes, such as need foolish hearers and slaves; for he will discern who are in them, and what concerns the nature of the numbers listed in them and assigned to each tribe; but we did not think it timely to set these things out now.

Let Celsus, and those who read his book, know that nowhere in the Scriptures received as genuine and divine are seven heavens spoken of. Nor do our prophets say anything they have taken from the Persians or the Cabiri; nor do the apostles of Jesus; nor does the Son of God himself.

title: The diagram of an obscure sect
english: Next, after the account he drew from the Mithraic mysteries, Celsus proposes that anyone who wishes should examine a certain rite of the Christians side by side with the Persian rite described before, setting them against each other and laying bare the Christian rite as well, and so see the difference between them. Now where he knew the names of sects to give, he did not hesitate to set out those he thought he knew. But where he ought rather to have done so, if indeed he knew, and to have taught which sect uses the diagram he sketched, this he has not done. It seems to me that here too he has set out the contents of the diagram in part, from garbled reports of a very obscure sect, the Ophites, I think.

We ourselves, in our love of learning, have come upon this diagram. In it we found the inventions of men of the kind Paul named, who make their way “into houses” and take captive “weak women burdened with sins, led away by various desires, always learning and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy 3:6–7). But the diagram was so wholly unconvincing that neither the easily deceived “weak women” nor the most boorish people, ready to be led by anything at all that sounds plausible, would have assented to it. At any rate, although we have travelled through many places of the earth and sought out those who everywhere profess to know something, we have met no one who championed the teaching of the diagram.

title: Leviathan, Behemoth and Gehenna
english: In it was a drawing of circles, ten of them separate from one another but bound together by one circle, which was said to be the soul of the universe and was named Leviathan. Of him the Jewish Scriptures, whatever their riddle may mean, said that he was formed by God as a plaything. For in the Psalms we found: “In wisdom you have made all things; the earth is filled with your creation. Here is the great and wide sea; there ships pass through, small living things with great; this dragon, which you formed to make sport of” (Psalm 104:24–26). In place of “dragon” the Hebrew has Leviathan. So the impious diagram said that the Leviathan so plainly condemned in the prophet is the soul that pervades the universe.

We found in it also the one named Behemoth, placed, as it were, after the lowest circle. The one who devised that foul diagram wrote this Leviathan on the circle and at its centre, setting down his name twice. Further, Celsus says that the diagram was divided by a thick black line, and he said that the diagram called this line Gehenna, which is also Tartarus.

Now since we found Gehenna written in the Gospel as a place of punishment (Matthew 5:22; 10:28), we searched whether it was named anywhere in the old writings, especially since the Jews too use the name. We found that in some places Scripture calls it the “Valley of the son of Ennom” (Jeremiah 7:31–32); but in the Hebrew, as we have learned, where “Valley” stands, “the Valley of Ennom” and “Gehenna” were used of one and the same place. Keeping close watch on the readings, we find also that Gehenna, or the Valley of Ennom, is listed in the lot of the tribe of Benjamin, in which Jerusalem also lay (Joshua 18:16, 28).

And as we examine what follows from there being a heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22), starting from the lot of Benjamin and the Valley of Ennom, we find something that bears on the teaching about punishments: souls of this kind are brought to a purification that comes through torment, according to the words, “Behold, the Lord comes in like the fire of a smelting furnace and like the washers’ lye; and he will sit smelting and purifying as gold and as silver” (Malachi 3:2–3)…

title: A teaching not for every ear
english: …and in keeping with the saying that around Jerusalem punishments come upon those who are being smelted (Ezekiel 22:18–22), those who have taken into the very substance of their own soul what comes from vice; and vice is somewhere called lead, in a figure. That is why, in Zechariah, lawlessness was sitting upon “a talent of lead” (Zechariah 5:7–8).

Whatever might be said on this subject is not for everyone, nor is this the time to set it out. Nor is it without danger to entrust a plain account of such things to writing, since the many need no further teaching than that about the punishment of sinners. For it is not useful to go up to what lies beyond it, because of those who, through fear of eternal punishment, barely check, even in some measure, the flood of vice and of the sins that come from it.

So neither the diagram nor Celsus knows the teaching about Gehenna. Otherwise those people would not have made so solemn a show of pictures and diagrams, as though they were presenting the truth through them; nor would Celsus, in his treatise against Christians, have inserted into his charges against Christians things in no way said by Christians, but by certain people who perhaps no longer even exist, but have wholly died out and dwindled to a very few, easily counted.

And just as it is not fitting for those who follow the philosophy of Plato to answer for Epicurus and his impious doctrines, so neither is it fitting for us to answer for what is in the diagram and for what Celsus says against it. Therefore we leave aside, as superfluous and set out to no purpose, what Celsus has said on these matters; for we ourselves will accuse those people more than Celsus does, before any who are held fast by such teachings.

title: An invented seal and an accursed God
english: Next, after what he says about the diagram, Celsus, without having even half-heard what members of the Church call the seal, sets out on his own some strange things and an exchange of words: that the one who puts on the seal is called father, and the one who is sealed is called young one and son, and answers, “I have been anointed with white ointment from the tree of life” (compare Genesis 2:9). We have not heard that this is done even among the sects.

Then he even fixes a number, said to be given by those who hand down the seal: seven angels, who stand on either side by the soul as it departs from the body, some of them angels of light, the others of those called “of the rulers”. And he says that the ruler of those called “of the rulers” is called an accursed god.

Then, seizing on the phrase, he rightly accuses those who dare to say this; and for this reason we too share the indignation of those who blame such people, if indeed there are any who call the God of the Jews accursed, the God who sends rain and thunder, the Creator of this world, the God of Moses and of the account of the world’s making that Moses gave.

But Celsus seems to have intended by this something not fair-minded, but, out of his unphilosophical hatred of us, utterly unfair. For he wanted to set against us those unacquainted with our teaching who read his work, as though we called the good Creator of this world an accursed god. And he seems to me to have done much the same as the Jews, who, when the teaching of Christianity first began, spread slander about the word: that Christians sacrifice a little child and partake of its flesh; and again, that those who follow the word, wishing to do the works of darkness, put out the light, and each lies with whatever woman happens to be beside him. This slander, against all reason, once held sway over very great numbers, persuading those who were strangers to the word that Christians are such people; and even now it still deceives some, who because of such stories turn away from coming even into the simplest conversation with Christians.

title: The Ophites are no Christians
english: Something of this kind, it seems to me, Celsus contrived when he set out that Christians call the Creator an accursed god, so that anyone who believed him when he says these things against us might, if possible, go so far as to put Christians to death as the most impious of all. Confusing the matter, he also sets out the reason why the God of the world’s making according to Moses is called accursed: he says that he is such, and deserving of a curse, in the view of those who hold these opinions about him, since he cursed the serpent that introduced the knowledge of good and evil to the first human beings (Genesis 3:5, 14).

He ought to have known that those who have taken the serpent’s side, as though it gave the first human beings good counsel, who outdo the Titans and Giants of myth, and who for this reason are called Ophites, are so far from being Christians that they accuse Jesus no less than Celsus does, and admit no one to their assembly unless he first pronounces curses against Jesus.

See, then, how utterly irrational Celsus has been, in his discourse against Christians, in treating as Christians people who will not even hear the name of Jesus, not even to hear it said that he was a wise man, or of modest character, or simply a man. What then could be more foolish or more mad, not only than those who chose to take their name from the serpent as the author of good things, but also than Celsus, who thought that the charges against the Ophites were charges against Christians?

Long ago the philosopher of the Greeks who loved plain living, and who set out a pattern of the happy life, showing that utter lack of possessions did not prevent him from being happy, proclaimed himself a Cynic. But these unholy men pride themselves on being called Ophites, after the serpent, the creature most hostile and most dreadful to human beings, as though they were not human beings, to whom the serpent is an enemy (Genesis 3:15), but serpents; and they boast of a certain Euphrates as the founder of their unholy teachings.

title: One and the same God
english: Then, in what follows, as though he were reviling Christians, accusing those who called the God of Moses and of his law accursed, and supposing that those who say this are Christians, he says: “What could be more foolish or more mad than this senseless wisdom? For what mistake did the lawgiver of the Jews make? And how is it that you claim for yourself his account of the world’s origin, or the law of the Jews, by means of some figurative allegory, as you call it, and yet praise against your will, most impious man, the Creator of the world, who promised them everything, who promised to increase their race to the ends of the earth and to raise them from the dead in their very flesh and blood, and who inspired the prophets? And then you revile him again? But when you are pressed by these people, you confess that you worship the same God; yet when your teacher Jesus and Moses of the Jews lay down contrary laws, you seek another god in place of this one and of the Father.”

In these words too this most noble philosopher Celsus plainly slanders Christians, saying that the same people, whenever the Jews press them, confess the same God as theirs, but whenever Jesus lays down laws contrary to Moses, seek another in his place. For whether we are in discussion with Jews or among ourselves, we know one and the same God, whom the Jews also worshipped of old and now profess to worship, and we in no way act impiously toward him.

Nor do we say that God will raise the dead in their very flesh and blood, as was said earlier. For we do not say that what is sown “in corruption” and “in dishonour” and “in weakness”, a “natural body”, rises such as it was sown (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). But on these matters we have spoken sufficiently earlier.

title: The seven archons of the Ophite diagram
english: Next he takes up again what he said about the seven ruling demons, who are never named by Christians but are, I think, accepted by the Ophites. And indeed, in the diagram that we ourselves obtained because of them, we found the order set out just as Celsus set it out. Celsus said that the first is formed in the shape of a lion, without stating what name these truly most impious people give him. But we found that that foul diagram said the lion-shaped one was Michael, the angel of the Creator who is honoured in the holy Scriptures. Again, Celsus said that the next one, the second, is a bull; the diagram we had said that Suriel is the bull-shaped one. Then Celsus spoke of a third, an amphibious creature that hisses horribly; the diagram said that the third is Raphael, the serpent-shaped. Again, Celsus said that the fourth has the form of an eagle; the diagram said that Gabriel is the eagle-shaped one. Then Celsus said that the fifth has the face of a bear; the diagram said that Thauthabaoth is the bear-shaped one. Then Celsus said that among them the sixth is described as having the face of a dog; the diagram said that he is Erathaoth. Then Celsus said that the seventh has the face of an ass and is named Thaphabaoth or Onoel; but we found in the diagram that he is called Onoel or Thartharaoth, and that he has the shape of an ass.

We too decided to set out such things exactly, so that we may not seem ignorant of what Celsus professed to know, and also so that we Christians may show that we know these things more exactly than he does, and know them as the words not of Christians but of people wholly estranged from salvation, who in no way call themselves by the name of Jesus, or of Saviour, or God, or Teacher, or Son of God.

title: The passwords at the gates of the archons
english: If anyone wishes to learn the inventions of those sorcerers as well, by which they wanted to draw people into their teaching as though they possessed certain secrets, though they were not really able to do so, let him hear what they are taught to say after passing through what they call “the barrier of evil”, the gates of the archons, bound for ever: “I greet the solitary king, the bond of blindness, heedless forgetfulness, the first power, kept by the spirit of providence and by wisdom. From there I am sent forth pure, already a part of the light of the Son and the Father. May grace be with me; yes, Father, may it be with me.” And they say that the beginnings of the Ogdoad lie here.

Next, as they pass through the one they call Ialdabaoth, they are taught to say: “And you, Ialdabaoth, first and seventh, born to rule with confidence, being the ruling word of a pure mind, a perfect work for the Son and the Father: I bring a symbol stamped with the figure of life, and I have opened to the world the gate that you shut for your aeon. Free once more, I pass by your dominion. May grace be with me; yes, Father, may it be with me.” And they say that the star Phaenon is in sympathy with the lion-shaped archon.

Then they think that whoever has passed Ialdabaoth and reached Iao must say: “And you, ruler of the hidden mysteries of the Son and the Father, who shine by night, second Iao and first master of death, portion of the innocent one: bearing now my own beard as a symbol, I pass by your rule, ready. By a living word you have overpowered the one who came forth from you. May grace be present, Father, may it be present.”

Next comes Sabaoth, to whom they think they will say: “Ruler of the fifth authority, mighty Sabaoth, advocate of the law of your creation, a creation being undone by grace, by a mightier pentad: let me pass, seeing the blameless symbol of your art, kept safe by the image of a figure, a body set free by the pentad. May grace be with me, Father, may it be with me.”

After him comes Astaphaeus, to whom they believe they will say such things as these: “Ruler of the third gate, Astaphaeus, overseer of the first source of water, looking on one initiate, let me pass, cleansed by the spirit of a virgin, seeing the substance of the world. May grace be with me, Father, may it be with me.”

After him comes Ailoaeus, to whom they think they are to say such things as these: “Ruler of the second gate, Ailoaeus, let me pass, as I bring you the symbol of your mother, a grace hidden by the powers of the authorities. May grace be with me, Father, may it be with me.”

Last they name Horaeus, and they think they are to say to him: “I have crossed the barrier of fire without fear. You who were allotted the rule of the first gate, Horaeus, let me pass, seeing the symbol of your power undone by a figure of the tree of life (Genesis 2:9), taken in an image after the likeness of an innocent one (Genesis 1:26). May grace be with me, Father, may it be with me.”

title: Names taken from magic and from Scripture
english: Celsus’s reputed learning, which is really meddling curiosity and idle talk, has drawn us on to these matters. We wished to show anyone who reads his book and what we have written against it that we are not at a loss about the lore Celsus learned, on which he bases his lies against Christians, who neither hold nor know such things, even though we too have chosen to learn these things and to set them out; so that the sorcerers may not, by claiming to know something more than we do, deceive those who are carried away by the show of these names.

I could also cite many more things and show that we know the teachings of the deceivers, but disown them as alien and impious and not compatible with the truly Christian doctrines that we confess even to death. Yet it must be understood that those who composed these things, neither understanding the things of magic nor discerning those of the divine Scriptures, mixed everything together. From magic they took Ialdabaoth and Astaphaeus and Horaeus; from the Hebrew Scriptures they took the one the Hebrews call Iao, and Sabaoth, and Adonaeus, and Eloaeus. But the names taken from the Scriptures are titles of one and the same God. Not understanding this, these enemies of God, as they themselves admit they are, thought that Iao was one, Sabaoth another, Adonaeus a third besides him, whom the Scriptures call Adonai, and Eloaeus yet another, whom the prophets name in Hebrew Eloi.

title: The flaming sword and the rite that leads nowhere
english: Next Celsus sets out other myths: that some people go back into the forms of the archons, so that some become lions, others bulls, others serpents or eagles or bears or dogs. In the diagram we had we found also what Celsus called “the square figure”, and what those wretched people say is at the gates of paradise. The flaming sword was drawn as the diameter of a fiery circle, as though escorted by the tree of knowledge and the tree of life (Genesis 3:24; Genesis 2:9).

Celsus, then, would not, or could not, set out the speeches that, according to the myths of these impious people, those who pass through each gate will make. But we have done this too, so that we may show Celsus and those who read this work that we know the end of that initiation which initiates into nothing, and know it as alien to the reverence toward God that Christians hold.

title: Celsus’s heap of misheard phrases
english: After setting out what was mentioned above and things like it (the things we ourselves have added), Celsus says this: “And they go on adding one thing after another: words of prophets, and circles upon circles, and emanations of an earthly church and of circumcision, and the flowing power of a certain virgin, Prunicus, and a living soul, and a heaven slain that it may live, and an earth slain with a sword, and many slain that they may live, and death coming to an end in the world when the sin of the world dies, and again a narrow way down, and gates that open of their own accord. And there, everywhere, is the tree of life, and a resurrection of the flesh from a tree, because, I suppose, their teacher was nailed to a cross and was a carpenter by trade. So if he had happened to be thrown down a cliff, or pushed into a pit, or strangled with a noose, or if he had been a shoemaker or a stonecutter or a smith, there would be above the heavens a cliff of life, or a pit of resurrection, or a rope of immortality, or a blessed stone, or iron of love, or holy leather. Or what old woman, crooning a tale to lull a child to sleep, would not be ashamed to whisper such things?”

In this Celsus seems to me to be jumbling together things he has misheard. For it is likely that whenever he heard some scrap of a phrase from any heresy at all, he did not make it clear even according to that heresy’s own meaning, but piled up bits of words and showed off before people who know nothing either of our teachings or of those in the heresies, as though he really knew everything that belongs to the Christians. The passage before us makes this plain too.

title: Where Celsus’s phrases came from
english: For to use the words of prophets is indeed our practice: we show that Jesus is the Christ proclaimed beforehand by them, and we prove from the prophetic writings that what the Gospels record about Jesus was fulfilled. To speak of “circles upon circles” perhaps belongs to the heresy mentioned before, which encloses within one circle, which they say is the soul of the universe and Leviathan, the seven circles of the archons. Or perhaps it is a mishearing of Ecclesiastes, who says: “Circling round and round the wind goes, and on its circles the wind returns” (Ecclesiastes 1:6).

“Emanations of an earthly church and of circumcision” was perhaps taken from the claim made by some that the church on earth is an emanation of a heavenly church and a higher aeon, and that the circumcision written in the law is a symbol of a circumcision performed there in a certain rite of cleansing. The followers of Valentinus give the name Prunicus to a certain Wisdom, in keeping with their own wisdom that has gone astray, and they want the woman who had a flow of blood for twelve years to be a symbol of her (Matthew 9:20; Mark 5:25; Luke 8:43). The man who jumbles together everything from Greeks and barbarians and those in the heresies misheard this and spoke of “the flowing power of a certain virgin, Prunicus”.

“A living soul” has perhaps been said in secret teachings by some of the followers of Valentinus of the one they call “the psychic demiurge”; or perhaps the soul of one who is being saved has been called, not unworthily, “the living soul” by some, to distinguish it from a dead soul. But I do not know of any talk of “a heaven slain”, or “an earth slain with a sword”, or “many slain that they may live”; and it is not unlikely that Celsus brought these in out of his own head.

title: Death abolished, the gates of righteousness, and the tree of life
english: “Death coming to an end in the world, when the sin of the world dies” is something we ourselves might say, when we explain the mystical teaching in the apostle, which runs like this: when he has brought “all the enemies” into subjection “under his feet”, then “the last enemy, death, is abolished” (1 Corinthians 15:25–26). And it is also said: “When this perishable puts on imperishability”, “then the saying that is written will come to pass: Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54).

As for “a narrow way down again”, perhaps those who bring in the passing of souls into other bodies will speak of it. And it is not unlikely that “gates that open of their own accord” was said by some who were hinting at and expounding the words: “Open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may go in through them and give thanks to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall go in through it” (Psalm 118:19–20). And again it is said in the ninth psalm: “You who lift me up from the gates of death, so that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Psalm 9:13–14). By “gates of death” the text means the sins that lead to destruction, just as, on the other hand, by “the gates of Zion” it means good deeds. So too “gates of righteousness” is the same as “the gates of virtue”; and these open readily to anyone who pursues the deeds of virtue.

As for the tree of life, someone will explain it at a more suitable time, when interpreting what is recorded in Genesis about the paradise of God, planted by him (Genesis 2:8–9). Celsus has often mocked the resurrection, which he did not understand; and now, not content with what he has already said, he says that “a resurrection of the flesh from a tree” is spoken of. He has misheard, I think, what is said in a figure: that through a tree came death and through a tree came life, death in Adam and life in Christ (1 Corinthians 15:22). Then, making sport of what is said about the tree, he mocks it on two counts, saying that it is adopted for this reason: either because our teacher was nailed to a cross, or because he was a carpenter by trade. He does not see that the tree of life is recorded in the writings of Moses (Genesis 2:9); nor does he see that nowhere in the Gospels current in the churches is Jesus himself described as a “carpenter”.

title: Celsus mocks the tree of life
english: He also thinks that we, speaking about the cross in a figurative way, have invented the tree of life (Genesis 2:9). And, in keeping with his own error on this point, he says: “If that man had happened to be flung down a cliff, or pushed into a pit, or choked with a noose, a cliff of life above the heavens would have been invented, or a pit of resurrection, or a rope of immortality.” And again he says: “If the tree of life was invented because he was a carpenter, it would have followed that, had he been a cobbler, something would be said about holy leather; had he been a stonecutter, about a blessed stone; had he been a smith, about an iron of love.”
Who, then, does not see at once how cheap his accusation is, when he heaps abuse on people whom he had undertaken to win back as people who were deceived?

Next after this he says things that fit those who invented the lion-shaped, ass-headed and serpent-shaped rulers, and anyone else who has told myths like theirs, but not those who belong to the Church. For truly, even a drunken old woman singing a child to sleep would have been ashamed to chant and whisper to the child a tale like the one told by those who invented the ass-headed rulers and the speeches, so to speak, made at each gate.

But Celsus does not know the teachings of those who belong to the Church. Very few have trained themselves to understand them: those who, following the command of Jesus, have devoted their whole life to searching “the Scriptures” (John 5:39), and who have toiled over examining the meaning of the sacred writings more than the Greek philosophers toiled to gain some supposed knowledge.

title: What the Ophite diagram really shows
english: Not content with what comes from the diagram, our noble friend wanted to put in some other things along the way, to swell his charges against us, who have nothing in common with it; and he repeated the doctrines of those people as though they were ours. For he says: “Not the least of their marvels is this: they expound certain things inscribed between the higher circles above the heavens, and among them two in particular, a greater and a smaller, of Son and Father.”

We for our part found in this diagram the greater circle and the smaller, on whose diameter was written “Father and Son.” Between the greater circle, inside which the smaller one lay, and another made up of two circles, the outer yellow and the inner dark blue, was the inscribed partition, shaped like an axe. Above it was a small circle touching the greater of the first two, with “Love” written in it; and below it, touching the circle, one with “Life” written in it. On the second circle, which was entwined with and enclosed two other circles and another figure shaped like a rhombus, was written “Providence of Wisdom.” Inside the area where those two overlapped was “Nature of Wisdom”; above that shared area was a circle in which was written “Knowledge,” and below it another, in which was written “Understanding.”

We have included these things too in our treatise against Celsus, to show our readers that we know, more clearly than he does and not from garbled hearsay, the very things that we too condemn. Whether those who pride themselves on such things also promise some magical sorcery, and whether this is for them the sum of wisdom, we do not affirm; for we have never come across anything of the kind. Celsus, who has often been caught already in false testimony and unreasonable accusations, may know whether he is lying here too, or whether he came upon something of this sort about certain people who are strangers and aliens to the faith and set it out in his own book.

title: Scythian names for the gods and magic charms
english: Then, against those who, as he says, use some magic and sorcery and invoke barbarous names of certain demons, he says something like this: that these people act like those who stage wonders with the same underlying realities before people who do not know that the names of those realities are one thing among the Greeks and another among the Scythians. Then he sets out, taking it from Herodotus, that the Scythians call Apollo Gongosyrus, Poseidon Thagimasadas, Aphrodite Argimpasa, and Hestia Tabiti (Herodotus, Histories 4.59).

Anyone who is able will examine whether Celsus, together with Herodotus, is perhaps lying about these things too, since the Scythians do not recognise the same underlying realities as the Greeks with regard to their supposed gods. For how could it be likely that Apollo is called Gongosyrus among the Scythians? I do not think that Gongosyrus, translated into the Greek tongue, yields the etymology of Apollo, or that Apollo, put into the Scythian language, means Gongosyrus. In the same way, no one will say the same about the rest either. For the Greeks, starting from certain things and etymologies, gave the names they did to those whom they regard as gods, and the Scythians started from others; so too the Persians started from others, and the Indians, the Ethiopians or the Libyans from others again, or named them in whatever way each people liked, since they did not hold fast to the first and pure conception of the Maker of the universe.

We have said enough about this in what came before as well, when we wished to show that Sabaoth and Zeus are not the same, and when we also set out something about languages from the divine writings. So we deliberately pass over these matters, in which Celsus calls us to repeat ourselves.

Then once more he mixes together things drawn from magical sorcery, and attaches them perhaps to no one, since there are none who practise sorcery under the cover of this kind of religion, or perhaps to some who use such things on the easily deceived, so that they may seem to do something by divine power.
