He sets out certain things, saying: “Why should I list all who have taught purifications, or songs of release, or cries to drive evil away, or clangings, or demonic figures, or every sort of charm against harm, made from clothing, numbers, stones, plants, roots, and in short things of every kind?” Reason does not require us to make a defence on these matters, since we are not in the least open to such suspicions.

title: A slander like the old lies about Christians
english: After this, he seems to me to do much the same as those who, out of their great hatred of Christians, assure people who know nothing at all about Christians that they have found out by experience that Christians eat the flesh of little children and have intercourse without restraint with the women among them. For just as these stories are now condemned as lies told against Christians, even by the multitude, people wholly foreign to our religion, so too statements like these of Celsus would be found to be lies: where he said he had seen, among certain elders who share our beliefs, barbarous books containing names of demons and wonder-working tricks. And he alleged that these men (these supposed elders who share our beliefs) promise nothing good, but everything for harming people.

Would that everything Celsus says against Christians were of this kind, so that it might be refuted by the great majority, who have learned by experience that such things are false, because they have lived alongside most Christians and have never even heard anything of the sort about them.

title: Magic has no power over those who pray
english: After this, as if he had forgotten that his task is to write against Christians, he says that a certain Dionysius, an Egyptian musician, who had spent time with him, said about the workings of magic that it has power over the uneducated and over people corrupt in character, but over those who have studied philosophy it can do nothing, since they have taken care to keep a healthy way of life.

Now if our present task were to discuss magic, we would have added a little on this point to what we said about it above. But since we must say what is more to the purpose in answer to Celsus’s book, we say this about magic: whoever wishes to examine whether even philosophers can be caught by it or not should read what Moeragenes wrote in his Memoirs of Apollonius of Tyana, the magician and philosopher. In them this man, no Christian but a philosopher, said that some philosophers of no mean standing were caught by the magic in Apollonius, having gone to him as to a sorcerer. Among them, I think, he told of the famous Euphrates and of a certain Epicurean.

But we affirm, having learned it also by experience, that those who, in the Christian way, worship through Jesus the God who is over all, who live according to his Gospel, and who use the prayers that have been commanded constantly and as they ought, night and day, cannot be caught either by magic or by demons. For truly “the angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them” (Psalm 34:7) from every evil. And “the angels” of the little ones in the Church, who are appointed to watch over them, are said “always” to behold “the face of the Father in heaven” (Matthew 18:10), whatever that face may be and whatever that beholding may be.

title: Celsus on Satan and the old myths of a war in heaven
english: Next, starting afresh from another point, Celsus says the following against us: “They also fall into some most impious errors, in connection with this very great ignorance, which has likewise wandered away from divine riddles: they make someone an opponent of God, and they name this same being ‘devil’ and, in the Hebrew tongue, ‘Satan.’ Besides, these notions are wholly the thoughts of mortals, and it is not even holy to say that the greatest God, when he wishes to do men some good, has someone working against him and is powerless. So, then, the Son of God is defeated by the devil, and, being punished by him, teaches us also to despise the punishments he inflicts. He foretells that Satan too will appear in like manner and display great and marvellous works, claiming for himself the glory of God, and that men must not be led astray by these and choose to turn aside to the other, but must believe in himself alone” (Matthew 24:24). “These are plainly the words of a sorcerer who is out for gain, and who guards himself in advance against those who hold rival opinions and gather rival crowds.”

Then, wishing next to set out the riddles which, he thinks, we have misheard and so bring in what we say about Satan, he says that the ancients hint at a kind of divine war. Heraclitus, for one, speaks thus: “One must know that war is common to all, and that justice is strife, and that all things come to be through strife and run their course” (Heraclitus, fragment 80). Pherecydes, who lived long before Heraclitus, tells a myth of army drawn up in battle against army: he makes Kronos the leader of one and Ophioneus of the other, and relates their challenges and contests; and they make a compact that whichever side falls into Ogenos should be the vanquished, while those who drive them out and conquer should hold heaven. He says that the mysteries about the Titans and Giants, who are reported to fight against the gods, also bear this meaning, and so do the Egyptian stories about Typhon, Horus and Osiris.

Then, having set out such things without explaining how those stories hold a higher meaning while ours are mishearings of them, he heaps abuse on us, saying that those stories are not like the ones about a daemon who is a devil, or (as is said with more truth) about a human sorcerer holding rival opinions. He takes Homer in the same way, as hinting at things like those in Heraclitus and Pherecydes and in those who bring in the mysteries about the Titans and Giants, in these words of Hephaestus to Hera: “For once before, when I was eager to defend you, he seized me by the foot and hurled me from the divine threshold” (Homer, Iliad 1.590–591); and in these words of Zeus to Hera: “Do you not remember when you hung on high, and from your feet I let down two anvils, and around your hands I cast a golden band that none could break? You hung in the upper air and the clouds, and the gods throughout high Olympus were indignant, yet they could not stand near and set you free; but whomever I caught I would seize and hurl from the threshold, until he reached the earth with his strength spent” (Homer, Iliad 15.18–24).

In explaining the Homeric verses he says that the words of Zeus to Hera are words of God to matter, and that the words to matter hint that from the beginning matter was in disorder, and God took it in hand, bound it together by certain proportions and set it in order; and that the daemons around it, as many as are insolent, he hurls away, punishing them with the journey down here. He says that Pherecydes, understanding these verses of Homer in this way, said: “Below that portion is the portion of Tartarus; the daughters of Boreas, the Harpies and Thyella, guard it; there Zeus casts out any of the gods whenever one grows insolent.” He says that the robe of Athena, which all behold in the procession of the Panathenaea, also bears such ideas. “For it shows,” he says, “that a motherless and undefiled divinity masters the earthborn in their arrogance.”

Having accepted the fictions of the Greeks, he adds, by way of accusing our teachings, that the Son of God is punished by the devil, and that he teaches us also to endure when we are punished by the same one. “These things too are utterly ridiculous. For it would have been right, I think, to punish the devil, and not to threaten the men whom he had slandered.”

title: Moses spoke of the fallen one long before the Greeks
english: See, then, whether the man who charges us with most impious errors and with having strayed from divine riddles is not himself plainly in error. He has not perceived that the writings of Moses, which are much older not only than Heraclitus and Pherecydes but even than Homer, brought in the account of this evil one who fell from the heavenly places. For the “serpent” (Genesis 3:1), from whom Pherecydes’ Ophioneus derives, and who became the cause of man’s being cast out of the divine paradise (Genesis 3:23–24), hints at something of this kind: he deceived womankind with a promise of divinity and of greater things (Genesis 3:5), and the man is said to have followed her (Genesis 3:6).

And the destroyer in Moses’ Exodus (Exodus 12:23): who else could he be but the one who causes destruction for those who obey him and do not resist his wickedness or struggle against it? Again, the one sent away in Leviticus, whom the Hebrew text named Azazel (Leviticus 16:8–10), was no other than he. The one that bore his lot had to be sent away into the wilderness and driven off to avert evil; for all who belong, through their wickedness, to the portion of the worse one stand opposed to those who are of God’s lot, and are deserts, empty of God. And the sons of Belial in Judges (Judges 19:22): whose sons are they said to be, because of their wickedness, if not his?

But more clearly than all these, in Job, who is older even than Moses himself, “the devil” is recorded as standing before God (Job 1:6; 2:1) and asking for power against Job (Job 1:9–12; 2:4–6), so as to surround him with the heaviest calamities: first the loss of all his possessions and of his children (Job 1:13–19), and second the covering of Job’s whole body with a savage elephantiasis, as the disease is called (Job 2:7). For I pass over what the Gospels say about the devil who tempted the Saviour (Matthew 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13), so as not to seem to bring proof against Celsus on the point in question from more recent writings. In the last parts of Job too, where the Lord spoke to Job through whirlwind and clouds (Job 38:1) the words recorded in the book that bears his name, one may find not a few things said about the dragon (Job 41:1–34).

I say nothing yet of the passages in Ezekiel that speak as though of “Pharaoh” (Ezekiel 29:2–3; 32:2), or “Nebuchadnezzar,” or the ruler of “Tyre” (Ezekiel 28:2–19), or of those in Isaiah where the king of Babylon is lamented (Isaiah 14:4–21). From them one could learn not a little about wickedness: what beginning and origin it had, and that wickedness came into being from some who shed their wings and followed the first who shed his wings.

title: How evil began, and who the Adversary is
english: For what is good by accident, as something added on, could not be good in the same way as what is good in its essence. Such goodness would never fall away from one who takes in, so to speak, the living bread (John 6:51) to preserve himself. If it falls away from anyone, it falls away through his own fault, because he grew careless about partaking of the living bread and the true drink (John 6:55). Fed and watered by these, the wing is restored, as the most wise Solomon also says, speaking of the man who is truly rich: “For he has made himself wings like an eagle’s, and he returns to the house of the one who is set over him” (Proverbs 23:5).

For it was fitting that God, who knows how to make due use even of those who have come to be what they are through wickedness, should assign such wicked beings a place somewhere in the universe, and should set up a training-ground for virtue, open to those who wish to strive “lawfully” (2 Timothy 2:5) to win it back. So, tested like gold in the fire (Sirach 2:5; 1 Peter 1:7) by the wickedness of these, and doing everything so as to let nothing counterfeit into their rational nature, they may show themselves worthy of the ascent to divine things and be drawn up by the Word to the highest blessedness of all and, so to speak, to the summit of good things.

He who in the language of the Hebrews is called Satan, and by some, in a more Greek form, Satanas, is, when translated into Greek, “Adversary.” Everyone who has chosen wickedness and the life that goes with it, since he does what is contrary to virtue, is a Satan, that is, an adversary of the Son of God, who is righteousness and truth and wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:30; John 14:6). But in the more proper sense the Adversary is he who, first of all those who were at peace and living in blessedness, shed his wings and fell from blessedness. He, as Ezekiel says, walked “blameless” in all his ways, until lawlessness was found in him (Ezekiel 28:15); and though he was “a seal of likeness and a crown of beauty” (Ezekiel 28:12) in the paradise of God (Ezekiel 28:13), as though sated with good things he came to destruction, as the word spoken to him with a hidden meaning says: “You have become destruction, and you shall be no more for ever” (Ezekiel 28:19).

These few things, then, we have set out boldly and at some risk in committing them to this treatise, though perhaps they amount to nothing. But if anyone with leisure for the close testing of the sacred writings were to gather from every part of them a full body of teaching about wickedness, how it first came to be and in what way it is brought to an end, he would see that neither Celsus nor any of those whose souls are dragged down and drawn away by this evil demon from God, from the right conception of him, and from his Word, has so much as dreamed of what Moses and the prophets meant about Satan.

title: Two extremes: Christ and the Antichrist
english: Since Celsus also tosses in, in passing, what is said about the one called Antichrist, though he has not read what is said of him in Daniel (Daniel 8:23–25) or in Paul (2 Thessalonians 2:3–12), or what the Saviour prophesied in the Gospels about his coming (Matthew 24:23–26), we must say a little about this too. Since “just as faces are not like faces, so neither are hearts like the hearts of men” (Proverbs 27:19), it is clear that there would be differences in “the hearts of men” both among those who have inclined toward the good, since they have not all been stamped and shaped toward it equally and alike, and among those who through neglect of the good rush toward the opposite. For among these also wickedness is poured out in great measure in some, and in others to a lesser degree.

What is absurd, then, in there being among men two extremes, if I may so call them, one of good and the other of its opposite, so that the extreme of good is in the man discerned in Jesus, from whom so great a conversion, healing and betterment flowed to the human race, and the extreme of the opposite is in the man discerned in the one called Antichrist? God, who has embraced all things in his foreknowledge and has seen what concerns both of these, willed to make these things known to men through the prophets, so that those who understand their words might be drawn close to the better and guard themselves against the opposite.

It was fitting that one of the two extremes, the best, should be proclaimed Son of God because of his surpassing excellence, and the one diametrically opposite to him the son of the evil demon, Satan, the devil. Then, since evil is most clearly marked as being at the outpouring of wickedness and at its height when it plays the part of the better, for this reason signs and wonders and powers of falsehood attend the worse one, through the help of his father the devil (2 Thessalonians 2:9). For beyond the help that demons give to sorcerers, who deceive men for the basest ends, there comes help from the devil himself for deceiving the human race.

Paul speaks about this one called Antichrist (2 Thessalonians 2:3–12), teaching and showing, with a certain reserve, in what way he will come among the human race, and when, and why. And see whether Paul does not set these things out with the greatest dignity, in a way that deserves not even the slightest mockery.

title: Paul and Daniel on the Antichrist
english: He speaks as follows: “We ask you, brothers, concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, not to be shaken from your mind or alarmed, either by a spirit or by a word or by a letter as if from us, as though the day of the Lord were already here. Let no one deceive you in any way; for [that day will not come] unless the falling away comes first, and the man of sin is revealed, the son of destruction, who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God. Do you not remember that I told you these things while I was still with you? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work; only the one who now restrains is still here, until he is out of the way. And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will consume with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearing of his coming. The lawless one’s coming is according to the working of Satan, with all power and signs and lying wonders, and with all the deceit of unrighteousness for those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved. And for this reason God sends them a power that leads them astray, so that they believe the lie, in order that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but took pleasure in unrighteousness” (2 Thessalonians 2:1–12).

To make each of these points clear does not suit the present treatise. But the prophecy about him is given in Daniel, and it can move one who reads with good sense and fairness to marvel at the words as truly inspired and prophetic. In them are told the things concerning the kingdoms to come, beginning from the times of Daniel and reaching to the destruction of the world. Anyone who wishes may read it; but see whether what concerns the Antichrist is not as follows: “And at the last of their kingdom, when their sins are coming to the full, there shall arise a king shameless of face and understanding riddles. And his strength shall be mighty, and he shall destroy marvellously, and shall prosper and act, and shall destroy the mighty and a holy people. And the yoke of his collar shall prosper; deceit is in his hand, and he shall be magnified in his heart, and by deceit he shall destroy many, and he shall stand up for the destruction of many, and shall crush them like eggs in the hand” (Daniel 8:23–25).

And what is said in Paul, in the passage of his that I set out, which says, “so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God” (2 Thessalonians 2:4), is also said in Daniel in this way: “And upon the temple an abomination of desolations, and until the end of the time an end shall be given upon the desolation” (Daniel 9:27).

It seemed reasonable to me to cite these few passages out of many, so that the hearer may understand, at least a little, the intent of the divine words when they teach about the devil and the Antichrist. Content with these on this subject, let us look at another passage of Celsus and contend against it as best we can.

title: Where the name Son of God comes from
english: After the passages set out above, Celsus went on to say something like this: “I shall show where they got this very idea of calling him Son of God. Men of old called this world the child of God and a youth, since it came into being from him. Very like each other, to be sure, are this child of God and that one!”

He supposed, then, that we speak of a Son of God by twisting what is said about the world, namely that it came into being from God and is his son and a god. For he was not able to attend to the times of Moses and the prophets and see that the prophets among the Jews foretold that there is a Son of God at all, before the Greeks and before those whom Celsus calls men of old. Nor did he wish to quote what is said in Plato’s letters, which we mentioned earlier, about the one who ordered this universe as being the Son of God (Plato, Letter 6, 323d), for fear that he too might be compelled by Plato, whom he often extolled, to accept that the maker of this universe is the Son of God, while the first God, who is over all, is his Father.

And if we say that the soul of Jesus has been united with so great a Son of God by the highest participation in him, and so no longer separate it from him, there is nothing to wonder at. For the sacred words of the divine writings know of other things too which, though two in their own nature, are reckoned as one and are one with each other. For example, it is said of husband and wife, “They are no longer two but one flesh” (Matthew 19:6); and of the perfect man, who is joined to the true Lord, the Word and Wisdom and Truth, that “he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

But if “he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit,” who has been joined to the Lord, to the Word himself, Wisdom himself, Truth himself and Righteousness himself, more than the soul of Jesus, or even nearly as much? If this is so, the soul of Jesus and God the Word, the firstborn “of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), are not two.

title: The Church as a body moved by the Word
english: Further, if the philosophers of the Stoa, who say that the virtue of man and of God is the same, say that the God who is over all is no happier than the one they count wise among men, but that the happiness of both is equal, Celsus does not laugh at the doctrine or mock it. But if the divine word says that the perfect man is joined and united by virtue to the Word himself, so that, rising by this line of reasoning, we do not separate the soul of Jesus from the firstborn “of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), he laughs at Jesus’ being called Son of God, not seeing what it is that the divine Scriptures say of him in secret and in a mystery.

In order to bring anyone who wishes to follow the sequence of doctrines and to profit by it to accept what is said, we say this. The divine words say that the whole Church of God is the body of Christ, given its soul by the Son of God, and that individual believers are members of this body, taken as a whole (1 Corinthians 12:27; Ephesians 1:22–23). For just as the soul gives life to the body and moves it, though the body is not by nature able to move itself with the motion of life, so the Word, moving the whole body, the Church, to what is needful and working in it, moves it and each member of those who belong to the Church; and they do nothing apart from the Word.

If, then, this has a coherence not to be lightly despised, as I think it has, what difficulty is there in holding that the soul of Jesus, or in a word Jesus himself, by that highest and unsurpassable communion with the Word himself, has not been separated from the only-begotten and firstborn “of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), and is no longer other than he? But enough of this here.

title: Celsus calls the creation story silly
english: Let us look also at what comes next, where he makes his pronouncement in a single phrase and, without saying anything even plausible, finds fault with Moses’ account of the making of the world, saying: “Moreover, the account of the world’s origin is also very silly.” Now if he had put forward the way in which it seemed to him silly, and some plausible arguments, we would have contended against them. But it does not seem reasonable to me to establish, in answer to his assertion, in what way it is not silly.

If anyone wishes to consider what moved us, and what we established, with what appeared to us a proof, about Moses’ account of the making of the world, let him take up what we have worked out on Genesis, from the beginning of the book as far as “This is the book of the generation of men” (Genesis 5:1). There we have tried, from the divine writings themselves, to establish what the heaven and earth are which came to be “in the beginning” (Genesis 1:1), and what is meant by the earth’s being invisible and unformed, and what the abyss is and the darkness upon it, and what the water is and the “Spirit of God” borne above it (Genesis 1:2), and what the “light” is which came to be (Genesis 1:3), and what “the firmament” is (Genesis 1:6) as distinct from the heaven made “in the beginning” (Genesis 1:1), and so on in order.

He has also pronounced the writing about the generation of human beings very silly, neither setting out the proofs nor contending against them. For he had, I think, no arguments able to overturn the statement that man was made “in the image of God” (Genesis 1:27). Nor did he understand the “paradise” planted by God (Genesis 2:8), and the life of man in it, which came first, and the life that came about through circumstance, when man was cast out because of sin and made to dwell opposite “the paradise of delight” (Genesis 3:24).

Let the man who says these things were told in a very silly way first attend to each of them, and to this one as well: “He stationed the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns, to guard the way of the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24). But suppose Moses wrote these things with no meaning in his mind, doing something like what the poets of the Old Comedy wrote in jest: “Proetus married Bellerophon, and Pegasus came from Arcadia.” Yet those poets put such things together because they wanted to raise a laugh; but it is not plausible that one who left writings to a whole nation, and wished to persuade those under his laws that these writings came from God, wrote what was irrelevant, and said without any meaning, “He stationed the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns, to guard the way of the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24), or any other of the things said about the generation of human beings and explored philosophically by the wise men among the Hebrews.

title: The days of creation
english: Next, having heaped together in bare assertions the differences in what some of the ancients said about the generation of the world and of human beings, he says that those who left our writings, Moses and the prophets, did not know what the nature of the world and of human beings is, and composed “profound nonsense.” Now if he had said in what way the divine writings seemed to him profound nonsense, we would have tried to overturn the plausible arguments that appeared to him to show that they are profound nonsense. But as things are, we too will do as he does, and jest, and pronounce that Celsus, who knows nothing at all of the nature of the meaning and of the word in the prophets, has composed profound nonsense and boastfully entitled it “True Doctrine.”

And since he brings forward as a charge, as though it were clear and precisely understood by him, the matter of the days of the making of the world, some of which passed before light and heaven, sun and moon and stars came to be, and some after these came to be, we will remark only this to him. Did it escape Moses that he had said earlier that the world’s making was completed in six days, and does he, forgetting himself, add to this: “This is the book of the generation of men, in the day when God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 5:1; Genesis 2:4)? But it is not at all plausible that Moses, with no meaning in his mind, said after the account of the six days, “in the day when God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 2:4).

And if anyone thinks that these words can be referred back to “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1), let him notice that “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1) was said before “Let there be light, and there was light” (Genesis 1:3) and before “God called the light day” (Genesis 1:5).

title: The days of creation and the borrowed light
english: But it is not our purpose now to give the account of things known by the mind and things perceived by the senses, and of how the natures of the days are divided between both kinds, nor to examine the passages one by one. For we would need whole treatises to explain the creation of the world as Moses tells it. This we did, as far as we could, long before the present treatise against Celsus, when, with the grasp we had many years ago, such as it was then, we discussed the six days of creation in Moses.

One should know, however, that through Isaiah the word promises the righteous that they will be in a state of day, in which not the sun but “the Lord” himself will be to them “an everlasting light, and God” their “glory” (Isaiah 60:19).

It was, I think, because he had misheard some wicked sect, which wrongly explained “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3) as spoken by the Creator in the form of a wish, that he said: “For the Creator certainly did not borrow light from above, like people who light their lamps from their neighbours.” And it was because he had misheard another, impious sect that he also said this: “If the one who made these things against the great God’s will was some accursed god opposed to him, why did he lend him the light?”

We are so far from having to defend ourselves against these charges that we want to accuse those people’s opinion of error more plainly still, and take our stand not, as Celsus does, against what we do not know of theirs, but against what we know accurately: partly from the people themselves, whom we have followed closely, and partly from careful reading of their writings.

title: The Spirit over the waters is not on loan
english: After this Celsus says: “For my part, as for the coming into being and the destruction of the world, whether it is ungenerated and indestructible, or generated but indestructible, or the reverse, I say nothing about this now.” So we too say nothing about these questions now, for the present treatise does not require it.

Nor do we say that the Spirit of the God over all came to be in the things here as in things foreign to him, on the strength of the words “The Spirit of God was moving over the water” (Genesis 1:2). Nor do we say that certain things wickedly contrived against his Spirit, as if by another, a Creator distinct from the great God, while the higher God put up with it, needed to be pulled down. So a long farewell to those who say such things, and to Celsus too, who accuses them without dealing with the substance. For he should either not have mentioned such things at all, or else, in keeping with what he takes to be humane, have set them out carefully and contended against the impious things they say.

Nor have we ever heard that the great God, after giving the Spirit to the Creator, demands it back. Then next, foolishly attacking impious doctrines, he says: “What god gives something intending to demand it back? For demanding back is the mark of one in need, but God needs nothing.” And to this he adds, as if saying something clever against certain people: “Why, when he lent, did he not know that he was lending to an evil being?” He also says: “Why does he look on while an evil Creator works against him?”

title: Celsus mixes sect with sect
english: Then, I think, mixing up sects with sects and not noting that these views belong to one sect and those to another, he brings forward the difficulties we raise against Marcion. Perhaps he misheard these too from some who attack that teaching cheaply and like amateurs, and not very intelligently at that. So, setting out what is said against Marcion, and without noting that he is speaking against him, he says: “Why does he send in secret and destroy the works this one has made? Why does he force his way in covertly, and entice, and lead astray? Why does he beguile those whom this one has condemned or cursed, as you say, and spirit them away like some kidnapper? Why does he teach them to run away from the Master? Why to flee the Father? Why does he adopt them himself, without the Father’s consent? Why does he profess to be the father of those who belong to another?”

And he adds to these words, as if in astonishment: “A fine God indeed, who longs to be father of sinners condemned by another, of the disinherited, and, as they themselves say, of refuse; and who could not avenge the one he sent to steal them away from the other, when that one was caught!”

Next after these, as if speaking to us who confess that this world does not belong to some foreign and strange god, he says something like this: “But if these are his works, how did God make evils? How is he unable to persuade and admonish? How does he repent over them when they have become ungrateful and wicked, and find fault with his own craftsmanship, and hate, and threaten, and destroy his own offspring (Genesis 6:6–7)? Or where does he lead them away to, out of this world which he himself made?”

It seems to me that here too he does not make clear what evils are, although among the Greeks too there have been many schools of thought about goods and evils. Instead he jumps to the conclusion that, on our teaching, God is the maker of evils, as though this followed for us, who say that this world too is the work of the God over all. Let the question of evils stand however it stands, whether God made them, or whether instead they came about as a by-product of what he primarily made. But I should be surprised if what he thinks follows for us, who say that this world too is the work of the God over all, namely that God has made evils, does not follow for him as well, judging by what he himself says. For one might say to Celsus: “If these are his works, how did God make evils? How is he unable to persuade and admonish?” And the worst fault in argument is to accuse people of other opinions of holding certain doctrines that are unsound, when one’s own doctrines are open to those very charges, and far more so.

title: What Scripture calls good and evil
english: Let us, then, for our part, look briefly at what the divine Scriptures say about goods and evils, and at what we should say in answer to “How did God make evils? How is he unable to persuade and admonish?” In the proper sense, according to the divine Scriptures, goods are the virtues and the actions that accord with them, just as evils in the proper sense are their opposites. For the present we shall be content with the words of the thirty-third Psalm (Psalm 34 in English Bibles), which establish this point as follows: “But those who seek the Lord will not lack any good thing. Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man who desires life, who loves to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 34:10–14).

For “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 34:14) is not said about bodily goods or evils, as some people call them, nor about external ones, but about the goods and evils of the soul. For whoever has turned away from evils in this sense and done good things of this kind, as one who desires the true life, would come into that life, “loving to see good days” (Psalm 34:12), days whose “sun of righteousness” is the Word (Malachi 4:2); and he would reach those days, as God rescues him “from the present evil age” (Galatians 1:4) and from the evil days of which Paul said: “redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:16).

title: God did not make vice
english: But we may also find bodily and external things called goods and evils in a looser sense: those that contribute to life according to nature are regarded as goods, and those that work against it as evils. It is in this sense that Job says to his wife: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10). Now in the divine Scriptures we find, in one place, God saying in his own person, “I am he who makes peace and creates evils” (Isaiah 45:7), and in another place, again about him, “that evils came down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem, the noise of chariots and horsemen” (Micah 1:12–13). These texts have troubled many who read Scripture, since they cannot discern what Scripture means by goods and evils. It is likely, then, that Celsus took his start from these texts: either he raised a further difficulty and said, “How did God make evils?”, or else he heard someone who held rather untrained views on this subject and set down the words quoted above.

But we say that God did not make evils, meaning vice and the actions that spring from it. For how could the preaching of judgment speak boldly, teaching that the wicked are punished for their vicious actions in proportion to their sins, and that those who have lived by virtue, or done virtuous actions, are blessed and will receive rewards from God, if God had made the things that are truly evil? I know well that those who want to venture the claim that these too came from God will take up certain texts of Scripture. They cannot show that Scripture is woven as one whole: Scripture that blames those who sin and welcomes those who do well, and yet no less says those other things, not few in number, which seem to unsettle those who read the divine writings without learning. I did not think it suitable to the present treatise to set out now the unsettling texts, which are many, together with their interpretations, which need much argument.

So God has not made evils, if one understands evils in the proper sense; but some, which are few compared with the ordering of the whole, have followed as consequences of his principal works. Just so, the curling shavings and the sawdust follow upon a carpenter’s principal works, and builders seem to make the debris that lies beside their buildings, a kind of rubbish falling from the stones and the mortar.

title: Pains that God sends to heal
english: But if someone means the things loosely so called, the so-called bodily and external evils, let it be granted that God has at times made some of these, in order to turn certain people back through them; what absurdity can the doctrine then contain? For suppose we loosely take as evils the pains that fathers, teachers and tutors inflict on those they are training, or that doctors inflict on those they cut or cauterize for the sake of treatment, and say that the father does evil to his sons, or that tutors, teachers or doctors do so: those who strike or cut would face no accusation at all. In the same way, if God is said to bring such things for the sake of the conversion and healing of those who need such pains, the doctrine would contain nothing absurd.

Nor would it be absurd if “evils come down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem” (Micah 1:12), evils that consisted in the pains inflicted by enemies and brought upon them for their conversion; nor if he visits “with a rod the iniquities” of those who have forsaken “the law” of God, “and with scourges their sins” (Psalm 89:30–32); nor if he says: “You have coals of fire; sit upon them; these will be a help to you” (Isaiah 47:14–15).

In this way we also explain “who makes peace and creates evils” (Isaiah 45:7): he creates bodily or external evils, purifying and training those who were unwilling to be trained by word and sound teaching. So much, then, for “How did God make evils?”

title: Why some are not persuaded by God
english: As for the question: “How is He unable to persuade and admonish?” It has been said already that, if this is really a charge, Celsus’s words could be brought against everyone who accepts providence. But one might answer in defence that God is not unable to admonish. For He admonishes those who listen, through the whole of Scripture and through those who teach by the grace of God; unless, perhaps, one were to give “admonish” some special meaning of its own, so that it also includes succeeding with the person admonished and his hearing the teacher’s word. But that departs from the sense the word commonly bears in ordinary use.

To the question: “How is He unable to persuade?”, which could likewise be brought against all who accept providence, this must be said. Being persuaded belongs, as it were, to the so-called reciprocal terms, like a man’s having his hair cut, where he acts by offering himself to the one cutting it. For this reason it needs not only the activity of the one who persuades, but also, if I may call it so, the yielding of oneself to the persuader, or the acceptance of what the persuader says. Therefore we must say that those who are not persuaded are not persuaded, not because God is unable to persuade, but because they do not accept God’s persuasive words.

One would not be wrong to say this of men too, those who are called “craftsmen of persuasion” (Plato, Gorgias 453a). For it is possible that even a man who has mastered the principles of rhetoric to the highest degree and uses them as he should may do everything to persuade, and yet, because he fails to win the will of the one who ought to be persuaded, may seem not to persuade.

And that, even if the speaking of persuasive words comes from God, being persuaded at any rate does not come from God, Paul teaches clearly when he says: “This persuasion does not come from Him who calls you” (Galatians 5:8). Of the same kind too is the saying: “If you are willing and listen to Me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are not willing and do not listen to Me, the sword shall devour you” (Isaiah 1:19–20). For if someone is to will what the one who admonishes says, and, having listened to it, is to become worthy of God’s promises, there must be the hearer’s choice and his assent to what is said. That is why it seems to me that this was said with emphasis in Deuteronomy: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, but to fear the Lord your God, and to walk in all His ways, and to love Him, and to keep His commandments?” (Deuteronomy 10:12–13).

title: Genesis says nothing of God repenting
english: Next we must answer this: “How does He repent over them when they have become ungrateful and wicked, and find fault with His own art, and hate, and threaten, and destroy His own offspring?” Here he slanders and misrepresents what is written in Genesis, which runs as follows: “When the Lord God saw that the wickednesses of those on the earth had multiplied, and that everyone was intently planning evil things in his heart all the days, God took it to heart that He had made man on the earth. And He considered it in His heart, and God said: I will wipe out man, whom I made, from the face of the earth, from man to beast, and from creeping things to the birds of the sky; for I am angry that I made them” (Genesis 6:5–7). He sets out what is not written as if it were made plain by what is written. For in these words no repentance of God is named, nor is it said that He finds fault with His own art and hates it.

But if God seems to threaten the flood, and in it to destroy His own offspring, we must say that, since the soul of men is immortal, the supposed threat is meant to turn the hearers back, while the destruction of men in the flood is a cleansing of the earth. So too those Greeks whose philosophy is not to be despised have said, in the words: “But when the gods cleanse the earth” (Plato, Timaeus 22d). As for the expressions that ascribe, as it were, human passions to God, we have said a good deal about them in the earlier parts as well.

title: Where the drowned were taken
english: Next Celsus, suspecting, and perhaps himself perceiving, what could be said about those destroyed in the flood by those who make the defence, says: “But if He does not destroy His own offspring, where then does He remove them to, out of this world which He Himself made?”

To this too we say that He by no means removes those who suffered the flood from the whole world, which consists of heaven and earth. But He frees them from life in the flesh, and, in releasing them from their bodies, He releases them at the same time from being on the earth, which in many places of the Scriptures is commonly called “world.” Especially in the Gospel according to John one can often find the region around the earth called “world,” as in: “That was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world” (John 1:9), and: “In the world you have affliction; but take heart, I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

If, then, someone takes “He removes them out of this world” to mean this region around the earth, nothing absurd follows for the argument. But if someone calls “world” the system made of heaven and earth, those who suffered the flood are by no means removed from the world so named. And yet a person who has understood the words: “while we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are not seen” (2 Corinthians 4:18), and: “For His invisible things are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that are made” (Romans 1:20), might say that one who is occupied with the invisible things, the things called, in a word, “not seen,” has gone out of the world, since the Word removes him from here and moves him to the region above the heavens (Plato, Phaedrus 247c) to behold the things that are beautiful.

title: Celsus repeats himself on the six days
english: After the passage we have examined, as though his aim were somehow to fill his book with many words, he says in other words much the same as what we examined a little earlier, where he said: “Far more foolish is it also to parcel out certain days to the origin of the world, before there were days. For when heaven had not yet come to be, nor the earth yet been made firm, nor the sun yet borne round in its course here, how were there days?” For how does that differ from this: “Further, taking it from the beginning, let us consider: how would the first and greatest God not be absurd, giving the command: Let this come to be, and something else, this or that, and on one day fashioning so much, and on the second again so much more, and on the third, the fourth, the fifth and the sixth?”

We have in effect already spoken also to the words “giving the command: Let this come to be, and something else, this or that,” when we cited: “He spoke, and they came to be; He commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 33:9; Psalm 148:5). We said that the immediate Creator, the one who as it were made the world with His own hands, is the Son of God, the Word, while the Father of the Word, by having commanded His own Son, the Word, to make the world, is Creator in the primary sense.

As for “the light” having come to be on one day (Genesis 1:3–5), “the firmament” on the second (Genesis 1:6–8), and on the third the waters “under the heaven” having been gathered into their gatherings, and so the earth having sprouted the things governed by nature alone (Genesis 1:9–13), and on the fourth “the lights” and “stars” (Genesis 1:14–19), and on the fifth the creatures that swim (Genesis 1:20–23), and on the sixth the land animals and “man” (Genesis 1:24–31), we have spoken as far as we could in our work on Genesis. And in the earlier parts too, when we found fault with those who, following the more obvious interpretation, said that a span of six days passed in the making of the world, we cited the words: “This is the book of the origin of heaven and earth, when it came to be, on the day that God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 2:4).

title: God’s Sabbath is not a tired workman’s rest
english: Then again, having misheard the words: “And God finished on the sixth day His works which He had made; and He ceased on the seventh day from all His works which He had made. And God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it He ceased from all His works which God had begun to make” (Genesis 2:2–3), and supposing that “He ceased on the seventh day” is the same as “He rested on the seventh day,” he says: “After this, indeed, like a downright bad workman, worn out and in need of idleness to rest.”

For he does not know what the day of the Sabbath and of God’s rest is, the day that comes after the making of the world, a making carried on for as long as the world stands. On that day those who have done all their works in the six days will keep festival together with God (compare Hebrews 4:9–10), those who, because they have left undone nothing of what fell to them, go up to contemplation and to the festal gathering of the righteous and blessed held on that day (compare Hebrews 12:22–23).

Then, as if either the Scriptures said so or we ourselves explained it so concerning God, that He grew weary and rested, he says: “It is not right for the first God to grow weary, nor to work with His hands, nor to give commands.” Celsus, then, says that it is not right for the first God to grow weary. But we would say that neither does God the Word grow weary, nor do any who already belong to the better and more divine order; for growing weary belongs to beings in a body. You may ask whether it belongs to those in a body of any kind whatever, or to those in an earthly body and one a little better than this.

But neither is it right for the first God to work with His hands; and if you take “work with the hands” in its proper sense, neither is it right for the second, nor for any other of the more divine beings. But let “working with the hands” be said loosely or figuratively, so that we may explain also: “The firmament proclaims the work of His hands” (Psalm 19:1), and: “His hands set up the heaven” (compare Isaiah 45:12), and anything said like these, when we take the hands and limbs of God figuratively. What, then, is absurd in God’s working with His hands in this way? And as it is not absurd for God to work with His hands in this way, so neither is it absurd for Him to give commands, so that the things carried out by the one commanded may be good and praiseworthy because the one who gave the command about them is God.

title: God has no mouth or voice, and does not change
english: Again Celsus, perhaps having misheard the words: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things” (Isaiah 1:20), and perhaps also because simple people have been rash in explaining such things, and not understanding what is meant when the names of bodily members are used of the powers of God, says: “He has neither mouth nor voice.” Indeed God will truly have no voice, if voice is struck air, or a striking of air, or a kind of air, or whatever else those skilled in these matters define voice to be. But what is called the voice of God is said, as the voice of God, to be seen by the people, in the words: “All the people saw the voice of God” (Exodus 20:18), “seeing” being taken, to use the customary language of Scripture, spiritually.

He also says: “Nor has He any other of the things we know.” But he does not make clear which things we know he means. If he means members, we agree with him, understanding “of the things we know” as those named in a bodily and more common way. But if we take “of the things we know” in a general sense, many things that we know are included; for God has virtue and blessedness and divinity. And if someone takes “of the things we know” in a loftier sense, since all things that we know are less than God, there is nothing absurd in our too accepting that God has none of the things we know. For what belongs to God is greater than all that is known, not only by the nature of man, but also by the nature of the beings who have risen above it.

If he had read the words of the prophets, David saying: “But You are the same” (Psalm 102:27), and Malachi, I think: “And I have not changed” (Malachi 3:6), he would have seen that none of us says that there is change in God, either in deed or in thought. For, remaining “the same,” He governs changeable things according to their nature, and His Word chooses that they be governed.

title: Where the image of God is found
english: Next Celsus speaks without having noticed the difference between “after the image of God” (Genesis 1:27) and “his image”: that the “image of God” is the “firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), the very Word, the very Truth, and also the very Wisdom, which is “the image of his goodness” (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26), while man has been made “after the image” of God (Genesis 1:27); and further, that every man of whom “Christ is the head” (1 Corinthians 11:3) is “the image and glory of God” (1 Corinthians 11:7). He speaks, too, without even having stopped to consider in which part of man the “after the image” of God is stamped, and that it lies in the soul that either never had or no longer has “the old man with his deeds” (Colossians 3:9), a soul which, because it does not have these, is called “after the image” of the Creator (Colossians 3:10). He says: “Nor did he make man his image; for God is not of this kind, nor like any other form.”

What sort of notion is it to suppose that the “after the image” of God resides in the worse part of the composite man, I mean the body, and, as Celsus has taken it, that the body itself is what is “after the image” of him? For if the “after the image” of God is in the body alone, then the better part, the soul, has been deprived of the “after the image”, and it lies in the corruptible body; and none of us says this. And if the “after the image” of God is in both together, then God must be composite, and must himself consist, as it were, of soul and body, so that the better part of the “after the image” would be in the soul, and the lesser, the part that answers to the body, would be in the body; and none of us says this either.

It remains, then, that the “after the image” of God is to be understood as lying in what we call the inner man, which is being renewed (2 Corinthians 4:16) and is by nature able to become “after the image of the Creator” (Colossians 3:10). This happens when someone becomes “perfect, as the heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48), and hears, “You shall be holy, for I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Leviticus 19:2), and, learning the words “Be imitators of God” (Ephesians 5:1), takes up into his own virtuous soul the features of God. Then too the body of one who has taken up the things of God into what is “after the image” is a “temple” of God (1 Corinthians 6:19), since he has a soul of this kind and, because of the “after the image”, has God in his soul.

title: God is shared in, not sharing
english: Once again he strings together a number of points, stating them as though we granted them, though no Christian of sense grants them. For none of us says that God shares in shape or colour. Nor does he share in motion: it is because he stands firm and his nature is steadfast that he calls the righteous man too to the same, saying, “But you, stand here with me” (Deuteronomy 5:31). And if some passages seem to describe a kind of motion in him, such as the one that says, “They heard the Lord God walking in the garden in the evening” (Genesis 3:8), we must understand such passages to mean that God is thought of as moving by those who have sinned; or we must understand them in the same way as when sleep, or anger, or anything of the kind is ascribed to God figuratively.

Nor, again, does God share in substance. For he is shared in rather than sharing, and he is shared in by those who have “the Spirit of God” (Romans 8:9). Our Saviour, too, does not share in righteousness; rather, being “righteousness” (1 Corinthians 1:30), he is shared in by the righteous.

The question of substance is a large one and hard to see into, above all if substance in the proper sense is what is stable and incorporeal. We would need to find out whether God is “beyond substance in dignity and power” (Plato, Republic 509b), imparting substance to those to whom he imparts it according to his own Word, and to the Word himself; or whether he too is substance, though he is called invisible in nature in the passage about the Saviour that says, “who is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), where the word “invisible” signifies the incorporeal. We must also inquire whether the only-begotten, the firstborn “of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), is to be called substance of substances, idea of ideas, and first principle, while his Father and God is beyond all these.

title: In what sense God is beyond word and name
english: Celsus says of God that “from him are all things”, though, I do not know how, he has cut all things loose from him. Our Paul, however, says, “From him and through him and to him are all things” (Romans 11:36), showing the beginning of the existence of all things in “from him”, their holding together in “through him”, and their end in “to him”. And in truth God is from no one.

But since he says, “Nor is he attainable by reason”, I distinguish the meaning and say this. If he means the reason within us, whether held within or spoken aloud, we too shall say that God is not attainable by reason. But if, having understood the words, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), we declare that God is attainable by this Word, and is comprehended not by him alone but also by anyone to whom he reveals the Father (Matthew 11:27), then we shall prove false the saying of Celsus, who states: “Nor is God attainable by reason.”

His “not nameable”, too, needs a distinction. If it means that nothing in words and their meanings can present the properties of God, what is said is true, since many qualities too cannot be named. For who can express in names the difference in quality between the sweetness of a date and the sweetness of a dried fig? Who can distinguish by a name and present the proper quality of each? It is no wonder, then, if in this sense God cannot be named. But if you take “nameable” to mean that it is possible to present in names something of what concerns him, so as to lead the hearer by the hand and help him grasp some things about God, as far as human nature can attain, there is nothing absurd in calling him nameable.
In the same way we shall also distinguish the saying, “For he has experienced nothing that can be grasped by a name.” And it is true as well that God is “outside every passion”. So much for this.

title: Darkness for idolaters, light for the Word’s followers
english: Let us look also at his next statement, in which he brings on stage, as it were, someone who, after hearing these things, says something like this: “How then am I to know God? And how am I to learn the way there? And how do you show him to me? For now you cast darkness before my eyes, and I see nothing clearly.” Then he gives what is meant as an answer to the one who raised this difficulty, and thinks he is supplying the reason why darkness has been poured over the eyes of the one who said these things. He says: “Those whom someone leads out of darkness into bright light, being unable to bear the brilliance, have their sight afflicted and harmed, and think they have been blinded.”

To this too we shall reply that all those sit in darkness and are settled in it who gaze at the wicked crafts of painters, modellers and makers of statues, and who refuse to look up and to rise in mind from things visible and from everything perceived by the senses to the Maker of the universe, who is light (1 John 1:5). But everyone who has followed the rays of the Word is in light. For the Word has shown from how great an ignorance and impiety, and from how great a want of learning about the divine, these things were worshipped instead of God, and has taken the mind of anyone who wishes to be saved and led it by the hand to the uncreated God who is over all. For “the people who sat in darkness”, the people of the nations, “saw a great light, and for those who sat in the region and shadow of death a light dawned” (Matthew 4:16; Isaiah 9:2), namely Jesus, who is God.

No Christian, then, answers Celsus or any of those who accuse the divine word by saying, “How am I to know God?” For each of them has known God, as far as that is possible. And no one says, “How am I to learn the way there?”, since he has heard the one who said, “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6), and has tasted, in walking it, the benefit that comes from walking it. Nor would any Christian say to Celsus, “How do you show God to me?”

title: Celsus’s darkness and the light that heals the blind
english: This, however, Celsus said truly in the passage before us: that someone who has heard his words, and has seen that they are words of darkness, answers, “You cast darkness before my eyes.” Celsus, then, and those like him wish to cast darkness before our eyes; but we, by the light of the Word, make the darkness of impious doctrines vanish. And the Christian might well say to Celsus, who says nothing clear or compelling, “I see nothing clearly in your words.” So Celsus does not lead us out of darkness into bright light. Rather, he wishes to move us from light into darkness, making “darkness light and light darkness”, and he falls under what Isaiah rightly said in these words: “Woe to those who make darkness light and light darkness” (Isaiah 5:20).

But we, since the Word has opened the eyes of our soul and we see the difference between light and darkness, choose in every way to stand in the light, and have no wish at all to come near the darkness. The true light (John 1:9), being alive, knows to whom its full brilliance should be shown and to whom only light; and, because of the weakness still in a man’s eyes, it does not display its own brightness to him.

And if we must speak at all of sight being afflicted and harmed, whose eyes would we say suffer this, if not the eyes of one held fast by ignorance about God and kept by the passions from seeing the truth? Christians, then, by no means think they are blinded by the words of Celsus, or of anyone else who is a stranger to the worship of God. But let those who perceive that they are being blinded by following crowds that go astray, and nations that hold festivals to demons, come to the Word who grants eyes, so that, like the poor and blind men lying beside the road who were healed by Jesus because they had said to him, “Son of David, have mercy on me” (Mark 10:46–48; Luke 18:35–39), they too may receive mercy and get back their eyes, new and beautiful, such as the Word of God would create.

title: How the Word makes the Father known
english: So if Celsus asks us how we think we come to know God, and how we shall be saved and brought to him, we will answer that the Word of God is able, when he comes to those who seek him or to those who receive him when he appears, to make known and to reveal the Father (Matthew 11:27), who was not seen before his coming. Who else can save the soul of man and bring it to the God who is over all, except God the Word? He was “in the beginning with God” (John 1:2), and for the sake of those who had clung to the flesh and become what flesh is, he “became flesh” (John 1:14), so that he might be received by those who could not see him in so far as he was “the Word,” and was “with God,” “and was God” (John 1:1).

And being spoken of in bodily terms and proclaimed as “flesh,” he calls to himself those who are flesh, so that he may first make them be formed after the Word who became flesh, and after this lead them up to see him as he was before he became “flesh.” In this way, once they have been helped and have climbed up from the first lessons according to the flesh, they may say: “Even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Corinthians 5:16).

He “became flesh,” then, and having become “flesh” he “dwelt among us” (John 1:14), not coming to be outside us. And having dwelt and come to be among us, he did not stay in his first form. He led us up onto the “high mountain” (Matthew 17:1) of the Word and showed us his glorious form and the brightness of his garments (Matthew 17:2), and not his own only, but also that of the spiritual law, which is “Moses,” seen “in glory” with Jesus (Luke 9:30–31). He showed us also the whole of prophecy, which did not die even after he became man, but was taken up into heaven; Elijah was its symbol (2 Kings 2:11). And one who has gazed on these things could say: “We beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

Celsus, then, has made up in a rather crude way what he thinks we will say to his question, how we think we shall come to know God and how we shall be saved and brought to him. But we would say what has been set out above.

title: The Son shares the Father’s greatness
english: Celsus, however, says that we answer with a likely guess, and he acknowledges that he is writing down our answer in this form: “Since God is great and hard to behold, he put his own spirit into a body like ours and sent it down here, so that we might be able to hear from him and learn.”

But in our teaching the God and Father of all is not the only one who is great. For he has given a share of himself and of his greatness to the only-begotten and “firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), so that, being himself “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), he might keep the image of the Father in greatness too. For there could not have been a well-proportioned image, if I may call it that, and a beautiful image “of the invisible God,” that did not also present the image of his greatness.

Further, in our teaching God is invisible because he is not a body; but to those who can contemplate him he can be beheld with the heart, that is, with the mind; and not with just any heart, but with a pure one (Matthew 5:8). For it is not right for a defiled heart to gaze on God; what would behold the Pure One as he deserves must itself be pure.

Granted, then, that God is hard to behold; yet he is not the only one hard to behold, but so is his only-begotten. For God the Word is hard to behold, and in the same way so is the Wisdom in which God made all things (Psalm 104:24). For who can behold, in each and every thing, the Wisdom in which God made each and every thing? It was not, then, because God is hard to behold that he sent the Son as one easy to behold.

Celsus did not understand this, and said, as though speaking for us: “Because he is hard to behold, he put his own spirit into a body like ours and sent it down here, so that we might be able to hear from him and learn.” But, as we have explained, the Son too, though he is hard to behold, since he is God the Word through whom all things came to be (John 1:3), also “dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

title: God is spirit, not body
english: If Celsus understood what we say about the Spirit of God, and that “as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God” (Romans 8:14), he would not have declared on his own, as though it came from us, that God put his own spirit into a body and sent it down here. For God always gives a share of his own Spirit to those who are able to partake of him; yet the Spirit does not come to be in the worthy by being cut off and divided. For the Spirit we speak of is not a body, just as fire is not a body either, which God is said to be in the words: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29; Deuteronomy 4:24). All these things are said figuratively, to present the nature of what is grasped by the mind by means of familiar and bodily names.

Just as, if sins are said to be wood and hay and straw, we shall not say that sins are bodies, and if good deeds are said to be gold and silver and precious stone (1 Corinthians 3:12), we shall not say that good deeds are bodies; so too, even if God is said to be a “fire consuming” the “wood” and the “hay” and the “straw” and every substance of sin, we shall not think of him as a body. And just as, when he is called “fire,” we do not think of him as a body, so when God is called “spirit,” we do not say that he is a body.

For Scripture is accustomed to call the things grasped by the mind “spirits” and “spiritual,” to set them apart from things perceived by the senses. For example, when Paul says: “But our sufficiency is from God, who also made us sufficient as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the spirit; for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:5–6), by “letter” he meant the sense-bound interpretation of the divine writings, and by “spirit” the interpretation grasped by the mind.

So it is, then, with “God is spirit” (John 4:24). Since both Samaritans and Jews were carrying out the commands of the law in a bodily way and in figures, the Saviour said to the Samaritan woman: “The hour is coming when neither in Jerusalem nor on this mountain will they worship the Father” (John 4:21); “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). By these words he taught that God must be worshipped not in the flesh and with fleshly sacrifices, but “in spirit.” Indeed, he himself may be thought of as “spirit” in keeping with the way one serves him “in spirit” and with the mind.

Moreover, the Father must be worshipped not in figures but “in truth,” which “came through Jesus Christ” after the law was given “through Moses” (John 1:17). For “when we turn to the Lord” (“now the Lord is the Spirit”), “the veil” that lies on the heart “whenever Moses is read” “is taken away” (2 Corinthians 3:15–17).

title: Not the spirit of the Stoics
english: Since, then, Celsus did not understand the things of the Spirit of God (“for the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned,” 1 Corinthians 2:14), he draws an inference of his own, thinking that when we say God is “spirit,” we differ in nothing on this point from the Stoics among the Greeks, who claim that God is a spirit that has passed through all things and holds all things within itself.

Now the oversight and providence of God do pass through all things, but not in the way the spirit of the Stoics does. And providence does hold within it all the things it provides for, and embraces them; but it does not hold them as a body holds, when what is held is also a body, but as a divine power that has embraced what it holds.

According to the men of the Stoa, who say that the first principles are bodily, and for this reason make all things perishable, and who come close to making perishable even the God who is over all, had this not seemed to them utterly absurd, even the Word of God, who comes down as far as men and the very least things, is nothing other than a bodily spirit. But according to us, who try to prove that even the rational soul is higher than every bodily nature, and is an invisible and incorporeal substance, God the Word, through whom all things came to be (John 1:3), would not be a body. He reaches not only as far as men but also to the things thought to be the least and governed by nature, so that all things may come to be through the Word.

Let the men of the Stoa, then, burn up all things in their world-conflagration; but we know of no incorporeal substance that is burned up, nor do we know that the soul of man, or the being of angels or thrones or dominions or principalities or powers (Colossians 1:16), is dissolved into fire.

title: Arguments that are not ours
english: So Celsus, as one who does not know the things of the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14), has spoken to no purpose when he says: “Since the Son is a spirit from God that has come to be in a human body, not even the Son of God himself would be immortal.”

Then again he muddles the argument to suit himself, as though some of us would grant not that God is spirit but that his Son is, and he thinks he meets this by saying: “There is no spirit of such a nature that it lasts forever.” It is as if, when we say that God is “a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29), he were to say: “There is no fire of such a nature that it lasts forever.” He does not see in what sense we say that our God is “fire,” and what it is that he consumes: sins and wickedness. For it befits a good God, once it has become clear, after each one has contended, what kind of contender he has been, to consume wickedness with the fire of punishments.

Then again he assumes, to suit himself, something we do not say: “It is necessary that God drew his breath back in”; and, as following from this, that “Jesus could not rise with his body; for God would not have taken back the spirit he gave once it had been defiled by the nature of the body.” It is foolish, then, for us to answer arguments as if they were ours, when they are not ours.

title: The virgin birth and the limits of sight
english: Next, repeating himself after saying a great deal in the earlier parts and mocking the birth of God from a virgin, to which we have replied as well as we could, he says: “If he wanted to send down a spirit from himself, why did he need to breathe it into a woman’s womb? For since he already knew how to form men, he could have formed a body around this one too, and not cast his own spirit into such great pollution. In that way he would not even have been disbelieved, if he had been begotten straight from above.”

He said this because he did not know the virgin and pure birth, without any corruption, of the body that was to serve the salvation of men. And though he sets out the Stoic doctrine, he shows no sign of having learned what it teaches about things indifferent, and thinks that the divine nature was cast into pollution and was polluted, whether by coming to be in a woman’s body until a body was formed around it, or by taking up a body. He does much the same as those who think that the rays of the sun are polluted in mire and in foul-smelling bodies, and do not remain pure even there.

Even if, on Celsus’s supposition, the body had been formed for Jesus without birth, those who saw the body would not at once have believed that it did not come from birth. For what is seen does not also announce the nature from which it came. Suppose, for instance, there were some honey not made by bees: no one could tell from tasting it or looking at it that it was not from bees. Just so, honey from bees does not show its origin to the senses; experience shows that it comes from bees. So too experience teaches that wine comes from the vine; for the taste does not tell us that it comes from the vine. In the same way, then, the body that is perceived does not announce how it came into being.

You will be brought to accept what I say by the example of the heavenly bodies. We perceive their existence and their brightness when we see them; but sense surely does not suggest to us whether they have come into being or are without origin. In fact schools of thought have arisen about these very things; and even those who say they have come into being do not agree on how they came into being. For sense does not suggest to them in what way they came into being, even if reason, pressing hard, finds that they did come into being.

title: Mockery in place of argument
english: Next he goes back over what he has often said before about Marcion’s opinion. In some places he sets out Marcion’s views truly; in others he has misheard even those. We need not answer that opinion, or even refute it.

Then he again brings up, on his own account, what can be said for Marcion and what against him, saying which charges they escape and into which they fall. And when he wants to side with the argument that claims Jesus was foretold, so as to accuse Marcion and his followers, he says plainly: “How will one who was punished like this be shown to be a child of God, unless it has been foretold about him?”

Then he jests again and, as is his habit, mocks, bringing in two sons of gods, one the son of the Creator and the other the son of Marcion’s god. He paints a picture of their single combats, saying they are like the fights of quails, and of the battles of their fathers, the gods; or else he says that the fathers, useless and doting from old age, do nothing to one another but leave their sons to fight.

So what he himself said earlier, we shall say to him: what old woman lulling a child to sleep would not be ashamed to say such things as he says in his book entitled The True Doctrine? For he ought to have stood up to the arguments in earnest; instead he leaves the substance aside and jests and plays the buffoon, thinking that he is writing mimes or lampoons. He does not see that such a way of conducting the argument works against his own purpose, since he wants us to leave Christianity and attend to his doctrines. Had he set these out with dignity, they might perhaps have been more persuasive; but since he mocks and jests and plays the buffoon, we shall say that it was for lack of serious arguments (for he neither had them nor knew any) that he fell into such great nonsense.

title: What Scripture says of his appearance
english: After this he says: “Since a divine spirit was in a body, it surely ought to have differed somewhat from the rest, in size or beauty or strength or voice or power to astonish or persuasiveness. For it is impossible that one to whom something divine belonged beyond others should differ in nothing from another. Yet this body differed in nothing from another, but, as they say, was small and ugly and ignoble.”

Here too it is plain that when he wants to accuse Jesus, he cites what comes from the Scriptures that seem to him to offer grounds for accusation, as if he believed them; but where, by the same Scriptures, one might think the opposite is said to what he takes up for his accusation, he does not even pretend to know it.

It is admitted, then, that it is written that the body of Jesus was ugly; not, however, that it was ignoble too, as he has set it out, nor is it clearly shown that it was small. The passage recorded in Isaiah, who prophesies that he would come among the many not in a comely form nor with any surpassing beauty, reads as follows: “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced before him as a child, as a root in thirsty ground. He has no form nor glory; and we saw him, and he had no form nor beauty; but his form was without honour, falling short compared with the sons of men” (Isaiah 53:1–3).

Did Celsus, then, listen to these words because he thought them useful for accusing Jesus, but pay no attention to what is said in the forty-fourth psalm (Psalm 45 in English Bibles), and how it is said: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one, in your comeliness and your beauty; and press on, and prosper, and reign” (Psalm 45:3–4)?

title: The prophecy and the Transfiguration
english: Let us grant that he did not read that prophecy, or that, having read it, he was led astray by those who misinterpret it as not prophesied about Jesus Christ. What will he say about the Gospel too, in which Jesus went up “onto a high mountain” and “was transfigured before” the disciples (Matthew 17:1–2) and was seen in glory, when also “Moses and Elijah,” “appearing in glory, spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem” (Luke 9:30–31)?

Or is it that, when a prophet says, “We saw him, and he had no form nor beauty” (Isaiah 53:2), and what follows, Celsus accepts that this prophecy refers to Jesus, blind as he is in accepting what is said, and not seeing that it is a strong proof that Jesus, who seems to be without form, is the Son of God, that even his appearance was prophesied many years before his birth; but when another prophet says that comeliness and beauty belong to him, he no longer wants the prophecy to refer to Christ?
