Now if it were clearly possible to gather from the Gospels that “he had no form nor beauty, but his form was without honour, falling short compared with the sons of men” (Isaiah 53:2–3), someone might have said that Celsus said these things not on the basis of the prophetic writing but on the basis of the Gospel. But as it is, since neither the Gospels nor even the apostles show that “he had no form nor beauty,” it is clear that he is forced to accept what comes from the prophecy as true of Christ; and that no longer allows his charges against Jesus to go forward.

title: The many forms of the Word
english: Again, the man who says, “Since a divine spirit was in a body, it surely ought to have differed somewhat from the rest, in size or voice or strength or power to astonish or persuasiveness”: how did he not see that his body differed according to what the beholders were able to receive, and was useful for that very reason, appearing such as it had to be seen by each? And it is not surprising that matter, which by nature is mutable and alterable, can be changed into whatever the Creator wills, and can receive every quality the Craftsman wills, should at one time have the quality of which it is said, “He had no form nor beauty” (Isaiah 53:2), and at another time one so glorious and awe-inspiring and wonderful that those who beheld such great beauty, the three apostles who had gone up with Jesus, fell “on their faces” (Matthew 17:6).

But he will say that these are fictions, no different from myths, like the rest of the wonders told about Jesus. We have already answered this at length in what came before. But the account also holds something more mystical: it declares that the different forms of Jesus refer to the nature of the divine Word, who does not appear in the same way to the many and to those able to follow him “onto a high mountain,” as we have explained it.

For to those who are still below and not yet ready to go up, the Word “has no form nor beauty”; for to such people “his form” is “without honour, and falls short compared with” the words that men have brought forth, which are figuratively called “sons of men” in this passage (Isaiah 53:2–3). For we might say that the words of the philosophers, which are “sons of men,” appear far more comely than the Word of God preached to the many, which also shows a “foolishness of preaching” (1 Corinthians 1:21); and because of the “foolishness of the preaching” that shows in it, those who look at this alone say, “We saw him, and he had no form nor beauty.”

But to those who, by following him, have received the power to keep up with him even as he goes up “onto the high mountain,” he has a more divine form. They see it, if anyone is a “Peter,” who has made room within himself for the building of the Church by the Word and has reached so firm a state that no gate of Hades will prevail against him (Matthew 16:18), since he has been lifted up, because of the Word, “from the gates of death, that he may” declare “all the praises” of God “in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Psalm 9:13–14); and they see it, if there are any who have received their birth from words of a mighty voice, and fall in no way short of a “thunder” that the mind perceives (Mark 3:17).

And “his garments” are different below: they are not “white,” they are not “as the light” (Matthew 17:2). If you go up “onto the high mountain,” you will see his light and “his garments.” The “garments” of the Word are the wording of Scripture; these words are the clothing of the divine thoughts. So as he himself appears different below, and when he has gone up is transfigured and “his face” becomes “like the sun” (Matthew 17:2), so too his clothing, so too “his garments.” When you are below, they are not bright, they are not “white”; but if you go up, you will see the beauty and “the light” of the garments, and you will marvel at “the face” of Jesus transfigured.

Consider whether it is not the same with what we learn about the Saviour in the Gospels too. For what concerns his birth, as his descent is traced from Abraham and he is “born of the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3), is “the book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ” (Matthew 1:1). But of the more divine and greater things that might be said about him and that he himself declared, John says that “not even the world, I suppose, could contain the books that would be written” (John 21:25). For the saying that “the world could not contain the books that would be written” is to be understood not, as some take it, of the number of the writings, but of the greatness of the matters; for the greatness of the matters not only cannot be written down, but cannot even be told by a tongue of flesh, nor expressed in human languages and sounds.

That is why Paul too, when he was about to learn the more divine things, came to be outside this earthly world of ours and was caught up into the third heaven, so that he might be able to hear the “unspeakable words” there (2 Corinthians 12:2–4). For what is spoken here, and is held to be the word of God, is told now that the Word has become flesh and, in respect of his being “God” “with God” (John 1:1), empties himself (Philippians 2:7). That is why we see the Word of God on earth as human, since he has become man; for in the Scriptures “the Word” is always becoming “flesh,” that he may dwell “among us” (John 1:14).

But if we lean back on “the breast” of the Word made flesh (John 13:25), and are able to follow him as he goes up “onto the high mountain,” we shall say, “We saw his glory” (John 1:14). Perhaps some others too, besides those who leaned on his breast and followed him “onto the high mountain,” will say, “We saw his glory,” but will not go on to add, “glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14); for this utterance befits John and those like him.

And by another, higher interpretation, those who have been able to follow close in the footsteps of Jesus as he goes up and is transfigured from his earthly appearance will see his transfiguration in each Scripture. It is as though the Jesus who appears to the many were the plain wording, while the Jesus who goes up “onto a high mountain” and is transfigured before very few of the disciples, and before those who have been able to follow to the heights, were the highest and loftiest sense, which holds the oracles of the wisdom hidden “in a mystery,” “which God foreordained before the ages for the glory” of his righteous ones (1 Corinthians 2:7).

But how could Celsus, and the enemies of the divine Word, who have not examined Christianity with a love of truth, know the meaning of the different forms of Jesus? And I mean also of his different ages, and of whatever he did before he suffered and after he rose from the dead.

title: Zeus in the comedy and the one corner
english: Next Celsus says something like this: “Moreover, if God, like Zeus in the comic poet, woke from his long sleep and wished to rescue the human race from evils, why did he send this spirit, as you call it, into one corner? He ought to have breathed it alike into many bodies and sent them out over the whole world. But the comic poet was raising a laugh in the theatre when he wrote that Zeus woke up and sent Hermes to the Athenians and the Spartans; do you not think you have made a more laughable thing of it, with the Son of God sent to the Jews?”

See here too how unseemly Celsus is. Quite unlike a philosopher, he takes up a comic poet whose business is laughter, and he compares our God, the Maker of the universe, with that poet’s Zeus, who wakes up and sends Hermes. We said earlier that God did not send Jesus to the human race as though he had risen from a long sleep. For good reasons he has now carried out the dispensation of the incarnation, but he has always done good to the human race. For nothing good among men has come about without the divine Word coming to dwell in the souls of those who were able, even for a short time, to receive such workings of the divine Word. Moreover, the coming of Jesus, which seems to have been into one corner, took place for good reason. The one foretold had to come to those who had come to know the one God, who read his prophets and were learning of the Christ proclaimed to them; and he had to come at the time when the Word was about to be poured out from one corner over the whole world.

title: One sun of righteousness, many anointed
english: That is why there was no need for many bodies to come into being everywhere, with many spirits like that of Jesus, in order that the whole inhabited world of men might be enlightened by the Word of God. The one Word was enough, rising as the “sun of righteousness” (Malachi 4:2), to send out from Judea the rays that reach the souls of those willing to receive him. And if anyone longs to see many bodies filled with a divine spirit, serving, as that one Christ did, the salvation of men everywhere, let him consider those who everywhere teach the word of Jesus soundly and with an upright life. The divine Scriptures call them christs too, in the verse: “Do not touch my christs, and do my prophets no harm” (Psalm 105:15). For just as we have heard “that antichrist is coming,” and have learned no less that there are “many antichrists” in the world (1 John 2:18), in the same way, knowing that Christ has come, we see that because of him many christs have come into being in the world. Like him, they have “loved righteousness and hated injustice; and therefore God, the God” of Christ, “has anointed” them too “with the oil of gladness” (Psalm 45:7; Hebrews 1:9). But he, who loved “righteousness” and hated “lawlessness” more than his “companions” (Psalm 45:7), received the firstfruits of the anointing and, if one may so name it, the whole anointing with the oil of “gladness”; while his companions, each according to his capacity, shared in his anointing too. Therefore, since Christ is “the head of the church” (Ephesians 5:23), so that Christ and the church are one body, “the ointment upon the head” has come down “upon the beard,” the marks of the full-grown man, the beard “of Aaron”; and this “ointment,” “coming down,” has reached “to the hem of his garment” (Psalm 133:2).

This too I have said in answer to the unseemly argument of Celsus, when he said: “He ought to have breathed it alike into many bodies and sent them out over the whole world.” The comic poet, then, to raise a laugh, made Zeus sleep, wake up, and send Hermes to the Greeks. But let our doctrine, which knows that God’s nature never sleeps, teach us that God orders the affairs of the world at fitting times, as reason requires. And it is no wonder if, because the judgments of God are great and hard to set forth, “uninstructed souls” go astray (Wisdom of Solomon 17:1), and Celsus with them. There is nothing laughable, then, in the fact that the Son of God was sent to the Jews, among whom the prophets had arisen, so that, beginning there in the body, he might rise with power and spirit upon the world of souls, which no longer wished to be left empty of God.

title: Celsus’s inspired nations and the Jews
english: After this Celsus saw fit to name the Chaldeans among the nations that have been most inspired from the beginning, and it is from them that the deceitful art of casting horoscopes has spread among men. He also ranks the Magi among the most inspired nations, and from them magic, which takes its name from their nation, has spread to the other nations as well, to the ruin and destruction of those who practise it. Earlier, even in Celsus’s own account, the Egyptians were in error, since they have stately precincts around what they consider temples, yet inside there is nothing but apes or crocodiles or goats or asps or some other animal. But now Celsus has seen fit to call the Egyptian nation too most inspired, and most inspired from the beginning, perhaps because they have waged war on the Jews from the beginning. And the Persians, who marry their mothers and lie with their daughters, seem to Celsus an inspired nation; so do the Indians, some of whom, as he said earlier, have even tasted human flesh.

But the Jews, and above all the Jews of old, who did none of these things, he not only did not call most inspired but even said would soon perish. He says this about them now as though he were a diviner as well, not seeing the whole dispensation of God concerning the Jews and their venerable ancient way of life, nor how “through” their “transgression salvation” has come “to the Gentiles” (Romans 11:11), and “their transgression is riches for the world, and their failure riches for the Gentiles” (Romans 11:12), “until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in” (Romans 11:25), so that after this “all Israel,” an Israel Celsus does not understand, “may be saved” (Romans 11:26).

title: Did God not know, and the close of the sixth book
english: I do not know how he can say of God: “He who knows all things did not understand this, that he was sending his Son to wicked men, who would sin and would punish him.” But it seems that here he has deliberately forgotten our teaching, which says that the prophets of God foresaw by the divine Spirit everything that Jesus Christ would suffer, and foretold it. From this it does not follow that God did not know that he was sending his Son to wicked men, who would sin and would punish him. Yet in the very next breath he says that our claim that these things were foretold long ago is something we say in self-defence.

But since our sixth book has reached a sufficient length, we will end the argument about here, and, if God grants it, we will begin the seventh. In it Celsus thinks he is answering our statement that the prophets foretold everything about Jesus. These matters are many and need a longer reply, and so we did not wish either to break the discussion off, forced by the size of the book, or, so as not to break off the argument, to make the sixth book very long and out of proportion.
